about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report, GAO-08-1005, examines (1) the changes and challenges described in the fiscal year 2009 overseas master plans, the extent to which they address prior GAO recommendations, and the plans' timeliness, and (2) the status of DOD's master planning efforts for the proposed military buildup on Guam. It is the fifth report on overseas master plans and the second on the Guam buildup, responding to congressional mandates that expired with DOD's May 2008 fiscal year 2009 report.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report finds that the fiscal year 2009 overseas master plans generally reflect recent changes in U.S. basing strategies and challenges, and address most prior recommendations, but DOD provided the plans to Congress in May 2008, 3 months after the February 2008 budget submission. The U.S. Pacific Command plan does not describe Air Force training challenges in South Korea despite a prior recommendation. DOD has developed a basic framework for the military buildup on Guam but has not issued its congressionally required comprehensive master plan, initially due December 2006 and extended to September 2008. The working-level plan slated for September 2008 is a one-time requirement and will not be a comprehensive master plan; the environmental impact statement and record of decision are expected in December 2009 and January 2010, respectively.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The report states: about 8,000 Marines and an estimated 9,000 dependents are planned to move from Okinawa to Guam by 2014; Guam's current population is 171,000, expected to increase by an estimated 25,000 active duty military personnel and dependents, or 14.6 percent, to 196,000; the total cost of all services' realignments on Guam is estimated to be more than $13 billion; the Marine Corps buildup is estimated to cost $10.3 billion; Marine Forces Pacific officials recently estimated the Marine Corps realignment alone will exceed $15 billion; training ranges for the Marine Corps in Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands are estimated to cost $2 billion; strategic lift operating from Guam will cost an additional $88 million annually; the government of Japan is expected to contribute a total of $6.09 billion, with up to $2.8 billion in funds without reimbursement and another $3.3 billion in loans and equity investments; the fiscal year 2009 military construction budget includes approximately $24.4 billion, of which nearly $1.1 billion (4.7 percent) is designated for specific overseas locations; U.S. European Command identified over $284 million in facility requirements for the ballistic missile defense program in the Czech Republic; U.S. Central Command identified a goal of $1.7 billion in host nation funding; the Japanese Facilities Improvement Program funding decreased from an estimated $1 billion in 1993 to $242 million; the U.S. government has received approximately $656 million in residual value and payment-in-kind compensation since 1989; the government of Guam will need $6.1 billion for infrastructure upgrades; annual construction capacity is estimated at $1 billion to $1.5 billion, potentially $2.5 billion with improvements, versus more than $3 billion per year needed; 15,000 to 20,000 construction workers will be required, with Guam able to meet only 10 to 15 percent of the labor requirement locally; the ballistic missile defense task force is approximately 630 soldiers and their estimated 950 dependents; DOD will require 500 defense civilians and contractors to support Marine Corps base operations.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends that the Secretary of Defense take two actions: (1) Direct the Under Secretary of Defense for Acquisition, Technology and Logistics to initiate a process of developing global defense posture updates earlier each year so that DOD can provide the congressional defense committees the overseas planning report with the administration's annual budget submission. (2) Direct the Executive Director of the Joint Guam Program Office to provide the congressional defense committees with annual updates of the Guam working-level plan until a comprehensive master plan is finalized and submitted to Congress. DOD partially agreed with the first recommendation and agreed with the second.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report notes that DOD has not yet fully identified funding requirements for the Guam buildup; the $13 billion estimate excludes costs for other defense organizations. It states that plans for the detailed force composition of units relocating to Guam, associated facility requirements, and implications for other services' realignments continue to be refined, and no decisions have been made on whether to deploy additional forces under the Grow the Force initiative. The report notes that the environmental impact statement and record of decision are not expected until December 2009 and January 2010, respectively, and will influence key decisions. It also notes uncertainties in the cost-sharing arrangement with Japan, including conditions that must be met before Japan contributes funds. The report states that DOD and government of Guam officials believe the schedule to meet the 2014 goal is ambitious given the possibility of delays in the environmental impact statement, the complexities of the move, and funding needs.

audience.name: Who it is for
audience.text: This report is intended for the congressional defense committees, to inform their oversight and funding decisions on DOD's overseas master plans and the military buildup on Guam.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report examines the fate of exported used electronics, the effectiveness of U.S. regulatory controls over their export, and opportunities for strengthening the federal role in regulating these exports, with a focus on the Environmental Protection Agency's enforcement of the CRT rule and the need for more comprehensive regulation.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: A substantial amount of exported used electronics ends up in countries such as China and India, where they are often handled and disposed of unsafely. Current U.S. regulatory controls do little to stem the export of potentially hazardous used electronics because the scope of regulatory control is narrow, regulatory controls are easily circumvented, and EPA has done little to enforce the CRT rule. The report found 43 U.S. electronics recyclers willing to export broken, untested, or nonworking CRTs in apparent violation of the CRT rule. EPA did not issue its first administrative penalty complaint until July 2008, and it has done little to ascertain the extent of noncompliance.

430 requests for central processing units; 665 requests for used computers; 230 requests for about 7.5 million used CRTs; over 60 percent of all requests; over 75 percent of the brokers' requests offered $10 or less per unit; almost half offered $5 or less; about 70 percent of the requests came from developing countries in Asia; 26 shipping containers of used CRT monitors intercepted and returned; $50,000 per day of violation; imprisonment of up to 2 years; 43 electronics recyclers; 64 responded; 343 solicitations; 25 companies submitted 47 notices for export of CRTs for recycling; as of July 2008, only 1 of these 43 companies submitted a notification; 18 of the 43 companies interviewed; 1,500 CRT monitors and 1,200 CRT televisions; 4 containers of CRT monitors (approximately 3,200 units); 20 containers (approximately 16,000 units); 900 as-is CRT monitors; two containers (900 units per container); 900 units; 1,100 and 1,200 monitors per container; $400; $10 to $30; 10 percent discount; 221 CRT monitors; 100 CRT monitors for $45; 155 CRT monitors for $366; 26 containers of 'waste' CRT monitors; six shipments (10 40-foot containers); 11 more days; 3 weeks later; $32,500 maximum civil penalty; 10 ongoing investigations (7 of which appeared to be from us); $4,000 to $7,000 per 20-foot container; $750 to ship 40-foot containers; $100; $1 a day; 80 percent of the natural resources; 1 metric ton of computer scrap contains more gold than 17 metric tons of ore; 4,000 tons of CRT glass leave the United States for the Malaysian facility each month; 250 shipping containers; 95 percent of the electronic items; 50 percent recycled-glass content; 2,234 requests; 430 requests; 665 requests; 230 requests; 7.5 million used CRTs; over 60 percent; over 75 percent; almost half; under $10; $5 or less; about 70 percent; 43 U.S. companies; 18 companies; 25 companies.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends that the Administrator, EPA, identify a timetable for developing and implementing a systematic plan to enforce the CRT rule, including enforcement targets, monitoring, follow-up of suspected violations, and prosecution. It also recommends that EPA develop options to broaden its regulations under existing RCRA authority to address the export of used electronic devices that might not be classified as hazardous waste by current U.S. regulations but have a high likelihood of threatening human health and the environment when unsafely disassembled, including expanding the scope of the CRT rule and revising the regulatory definition of hazardous waste. Additionally, it recommends that EPA cooperate with other federal agencies to improve the tracking of exported used electronics, which could be accomplished by implementing specific harmonized tariff codes for these devices. Finally, it recommends that EPA submit to Congress a legislative package for ratification of the Basel Convention.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report notes that EPA has not yet implemented the 2001 OECD decision, and that the legislative package for Basel Convention ratification has not been submitted to Congress. It also notes that the outcome of EPA's investigation into the containers intercepted and returned by Hong Kong was pending, and that the outcome of EPA's investigation into the shipment returned to the Port of Tacoma was pending. The report acknowledges that some government and industry officials have expressed concerns about some aspects of the Basel Convention, including lingering uncertainties over definitions of exports for recycling, refurbishment, and reuse, and that disagreement persists among Basel parties on these issues.

audience.text: The report is addressed to the Committee on Foreign Affairs, House of Representatives, and supports congressional oversight and decision-making regarding U.S. regulation and enforcement of used electronics exports.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a GAO report (GAO-08-1075R) that identifies, for each of the 18 critical infrastructure sectors, the federal laws, regulations, and mandatory standards that pertain to securing privately owned information technology systems and data, and identifies the enforcement mechanisms for each of those requirements. It summarizes findings from a briefing presented to House Homeland Security subcommittees on July 24, 2008.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report identifies at least 34 federal laws, regulations, and mandatory standards that pertain to securing privately owned IT systems and data in critical infrastructure sectors: 1 law, 25 regulations, and 8 mandatory standards. These requirements apply in 10 of the 18 sectors. Eight sectors did not identify any such requirements: critical manufacturing, defense industrial base, emergency services, government facilities, information technology, national monuments and icons, postal and shipping, and telecommunications. Each of the 34 requirements has at least one enforcement mechanism, including court injunctions, civil monetary penalties, criminal penalties, and administrative actions.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: At least 34 federal laws, regulations, and mandatory standards; 1 law, 25 regulations, 8 mandatory standards; requirements pertain to 10 of 18 critical infrastructure sectors. By sector: agriculture and food 1 regulation; banking and finance 17 regulations; chemical 1 regulation; commercial facilities 1 regulation; dams 8 mandatory standards; drinking water and water treatment systems 1 law; energy 1 regulation and 8 mandatory standards; nuclear reactors, materials, and waste 1 regulation; public health and healthcare 1 regulation; transportation systems 2 regulations. Civil monetary penalty up to $1 million per day for banking and finance; community water system fine up to $25,000 per violation; entity in nuclear sector fined up to $100,000 per day per violation; agriculture and food penalty of imprisonment up to one year, a fine up to $1,000, or both; chemical facility fined up to $25,000 per day; tribal operator fined up to $25,000 per violation in commercial facilities; public health and healthcare fine up to $50,000 and imprisonment up to 1 year; transportation systems fine up to $100,000 per violation.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document makes one recommendation: in October 2007, GAO reported that each critical infrastructure sector addressed key aspects of cyber security in its sector-specific plan to varying degrees, and recommended that the Secretary of Homeland Security request that, by September 2008, the sector-specific agencies develop plans that address all key aspects.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report notes that agencies may not have identified all applicable requirements because GAO did not conduct an independent search for applicable requirements. The review did not include privately owned IT systems operated on behalf of a federal agency, such as contractor systems subject to FISMA. The enforcement mechanisms identified are examples and do not necessarily constitute a complete list. The document states that for the chemical sector, the risk-based performance standards have not been finalized or submitted for approval, and therefore are not yet enforceable.

audience.name: Who it is for
audience.text: The audience is the Chairmen and staffs of the House Homeland Security Subcommittees on Emerging Threats, Cybersecurity, and Science and Technology and on Transportation Security and Infrastructure Protection, and other interested congressional committees and parties.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report assesses the Federal Aviation Administration's ability to acquire and integrate new air traffic control systems and transition to the Next Generation Air Transportation System (NextGen), covering the status and outcomes of ATC system acquisitions, key NextGen planning and transition issues, and key challenges FAA faces in implementing NextGen.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: Most of FAA's major ATC acquisition programs are being managed within established cost and time estimates since the creation of its performance-based Air Traffic Organization (ATO) in 2004. For example, 24 major acquisition programs experienced a cumulative 2.5 percent cost underage and only a 2.7 percent schedule overage when the baseline status as of February 2004 was compared to the estimated total cost and schedule as of June 2008. However, FAA measures progress related to current program baselines, and the agency will need to ensure transparency so that rebaselined programs and performance reporting do not mask budget increases and schedule delays. JPDO has completed the initial versions of three basic planning documents for NextGen—a Concept of Operations, an Enterprise Architecture, and an Integrated Work Plan—and ATO recently reorganized to facilitate the transition to NextGen, but industry stakeholders have concerns about both efforts. Many aviation industry stakeholders were not satisfied with the impact of their participation in NextGen planning and felt that the planning documents lacked the information the industry needed for NextGen to be implemented by 2025. All 10 stakeholders who discussed FAA's management structure believed that it was not adequate for the transition to NextGen, with multiple executives responsible for NextGen-related activities and the lack of a single manager with authority to make key decisions. FAA's ability to implement NextGen will be affected by how well it addresses key challenges, including research and development, human capital, and infrastructure. Research and development is still needed to define and demonstrate new NextGen technology, but it is uncertain which entities will fund and conduct that research. FAA faces a human capital challenge of having the necessary knowledge and skills, such as systems engineers and contract management expertise, to implement NextGen. FAA also faces an immediate challenge to maintain and repair existing infrastructure to keep the current ATC system operating safely, while managing its resources to develop facilities that can accommodate NextGen technology and operations. The agency has not developed a cost analysis or implementation plan for reconfiguring its facilities. Even with planned runway improvements and the additional capacity gained through NextGen technologies and procedures, FAA analyses indicate that 14 more airports will still need additional capacity.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: 24 major acquisition programs experienced a cumulative 2.5 percent cost underage and only a 2.7 percent schedule overage (February 2004 to June 2008). One in four flights faces delays. The U.S. air transportation system handles about 50,000 flights over a 24-hour period. By 2025, air traffic is projected to increase two-to three-fold, equating to about 100,000 to 150,000 flights every 24 hours. In 2007, 27 percent of flights were delayed or canceled. Delays cost passengers, airlines, and the U.S. economy over $40 billion. FAA plans to spend roughly $5.4 billion from fiscal years 2009 through 2013 on NextGen development and capital costs. The agency estimates that the total federal cost for NextGen infrastructure through 2025 will range from $15 billion to $22 billion. JPDO reported in 2006 that the total cost for NextGen infrastructure may range from $15 billion to $22 billion, with a corresponding cost to system users in the range of $14 billion to $20 billion. Acquisitions on which FAA reported performance from 2003 to 2006 collectively exceeded their original budget estimates by approximately $4.4 billion, or over 66 percent, and experienced schedule slippages of from 1 to 10 years. NASA's aeronautics research budget declined from about $959 million in 2004 to $511 million in 2008. About $280 million of NASA's proposed $447 million aeronautics research budget proposed for fiscal year 2009 would contribute to NextGen efforts. FAA will spend an estimated $740 million on NextGen-related research and development during fiscal years 2009 through 2013. The administration's proposed budget for fiscal year 2009 requests $56.5 million for FAA research and development to support the integration and implementation of NextGen programs, a substantial increase over the $24.3 million authorized for fiscal year 2008. Proposed legislation would provide $111 million for fiscal years 2009 through 2011 for a new FAA program to help close the research and development gap and reduce aviation noise and emissions. FAA plans to invest $180.4 million in human factors research from fiscal year 2009 to fiscal year 2013. FAA estimates it could need 150 to 200 more staff. FAA is responsible for maintaining over 400 terminal facilities. The agency rated the average condition of 89 of them as 'fair,' with some rated 'good' and others 'very poor.' Based on its assessment of these 89 facilities, FAA estimated that a onetime cost of repair to all of its terminal facilities would range from $250 million to $350 million. By 2025, 14 airports will still need additional capacity. The 14 airports are: Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International; Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International; John F. Kennedy International; John Wayne-Orange County; LaGuardia; Long Beach-Daugherty Field; McCarran International; Metropolitan Oakland International; Midway; Newark Liberty International; Philadelphia International; Phoenix Sky Harbor International; San Diego International; San Francisco International.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document recommends that FAA identify or establish a vehicle for regularly reporting to Congress and the public on the agency's overall, long-term performance in acquiring ATC systems by providing original budget and schedule baselines for each rebaselined program and the reasons for the rebaselining. It also recommends that FAA report information on the potential effects that any budget increases or schedule slippages could have on the overall transition to NextGen. FAA plans to address this by reporting such information in its Capital Improvement Plan, which it sends annually to Congress.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that it is too early to tell if the May 2008 reorganization of ATO sufficiently addresses concerns raised by stakeholders about the fragmented management structure for NextGen. It is also too early to tell if the reorganization will affect JPDO's overall role or its ability to coordinate and act as an honest broker among the federal partners. It is uncertain which entities will fund and conduct the research and development needed for NextGen. JPDO has not yet determined what NextGen research and development needs to be done first and at what cost to demonstrate and integrate NextGen technologies into the national airspace system. It remains to be seen if FAA's planned research and development in human factors will offset NASA's reductions. FAA has not developed a comprehensive plan to reconfigure its facilities, and the cost analysis has not been completed. Until the cost analysis is completed and the reconfiguration plan has been developed, the configurations needed for NextGen cannot be implemented and potential savings that could help offset the cost of NextGen will not be realized. FAA has not assessed the physical condition of all of its terminal facilities. The document also notes that the Senate Appropriations Committee has expressed concern that the JPDO planning documents lack details on how the various NextGen initiatives will reduce delays and congestion between now and 2025.

audience.name: Who it is for
audience.text: This report is for Congress and other federal decision makers, as it is addressed to Congressional requesters and sent to the Secretaries of Transportation, Defense, Commerce, and Homeland Security and the Administrators of NASA and FAA.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a GAO report, GAO-08-1123, issued September 18, 2008, to Congressional Requesters, examining the collaboration between the Small Business Administration (SBA) and the USDA Rural Development offices. It assesses the rationale for collaboration based on complementary programs, reviews past and current collaborative efforts, and identifies opportunities to improve collaboration. The report includes program descriptions, comparative analysis, findings on collaboration frequency and formality, and recommendations.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The document finds that the complementary nature of some SBA and Rural Development programs provides a rationale for collaboration, and that both agencies share similar missions and serve similar rural areas. However, collaborative efforts have been sporadic, mostly initiated at the local level, and dependent on established working relationships. A query showed that about half of SBA's 68 district offices and about half of Rural Development's 47 state offices reported ongoing collaborative efforts. The document also finds that SBA and Rural Development lack formal incentives for collaboration and do not track results, and that the December 2000 MOU was not effectively implemented when active.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: In fiscal year 2007: 7(a) provided more than 99,000 loans totaling nearly $14 billion; 504 provided about 11,000 loans totaling approximately $6 billion; 7(m) provided about $19 million in microloans; SBIC provided over $2.5 billion to more than 2,000 small businesses; B&I provided over $836 million in loan guarantees; IRP totaled about $34 million; RBEG approximately $43 million in grants; RBOG about $7 million in funding; REDLG about $26 million in loans and about $10 million in grants; renewable energy about $48 million in energy loans and $11 million in energy grants, with over $18 million in joint funding. Maximum loan amounts: SBA 7(a) $2 million; B&I $25 million. Maximum guaranty: 7(a) 85% for loans up to $150,000, 75% for loans over $150,000; B&I 80% for loans up to $5 million, 70% for loans between $5 million and $10 million, 60% for loans over $10 million. SBA processes loans in 5 to 7 business days, Rural Development 10 to 60 days. SBA has 68 field offices, Rural Development has 47 state offices and about 500 field offices, and more than 950 SBDC locations. In fiscal year 2007, IRP spending totaled about $34 million; 504 program about 11,000 loans totaling approximately $6 billion; and the Small/Rural Lender Advantage Pilot Program guarantees 85% of loans up to $150,000 and 75% above $150,000.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document recommends that the Administrator of SBA and Secretary of Agriculture take steps to adopt a formal approach to encourage further collaboration in support of common economic development goals in rural areas. Such steps could include establishing and implementing a written agreement, defining and articulating a common outcome, specifying roles and responsibilities, establishing mechanisms to monitor, evaluate, and report on results, and reinforcing accountability for collaborative efforts.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document notes that collaboration between SBA and Rural Development is not specifically required by law or regulation, and that officials were not able to provide examples of formal or informal efforts at the outset of the review. It also reports that the December 2000 MOU expired in 2003 and was not renewed, and that neither agency appeared to monitor collaboration implementation. The document states that the agencies do not track the results of collaborative efforts, and that some officials were unfamiliar with the MOU.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a September 2008 U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO) report to a Senate subcommittee. It provides a follow-up assessment of the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and its Office of the National Coordinator for Health IT's efforts to define and implement an overall privacy approach for protecting electronic personal health information exchanged within a nationwide health information network. The scope covers identifying milestones and responsible entities, addressing key HIPAA privacy principles, and addressing challenges to nationwide health information exchange, concluding that HHS has taken important steps but more work remains.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: HHS has fulfilled the first part of GAO's January 2007 recommendation by identifying milestones and the entity responsible for integrating the outcomes of its privacy-related initiatives. HHS has taken important steps in addressing the other two parts, including initiatives such as standards development, certification criteria, and state-level collaborations. However, HHS has not fully implemented an overall privacy approach because it has not defined a process for ensuring that all privacy principles and challenges will be fully and adequately addressed. The absence of such a process poses a risk that privacy protection measures may not be consistently and effectively built into health IT programs, potentially jeopardizing patient privacy and public confidence and trust.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: Nearly 60 percent of respondents to a September 2007 Institute of Medicine survey did not believe privacy of personal medical records and health information was adequately protected. HHS awarded four health IT contracts in 2005. The federal health IT strategic plan was released in June 2008, including target dates such as completing a confidentiality, privacy, and security framework by the end of 2008 and addressing inconsistent statutes or regulations by the end of 2011. The National Coordinator indicated the framework is to be developed and published by the end of calendar year 2008.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: GAO recommends that the Secretary of Health and Human Services direct the National Coordinator for Health IT to include in the department's overall privacy approach a process for assessing and prioritizing its many privacy-related initiatives and the needs of stakeholders to ensure that key privacy principles and challenges are completely and adequately addressed.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that HHS has not defined a process for ensuring that all privacy principles and challenges will be fully and adequately addressed. It also notes that without such a process, some principles and challenges may be addressed extensively while others may receive inadequate attention, leading to gaps in coverage. The document mentions that recommendations from advisory groups are still under consideration by the Secretary, and that HHS neither agreed nor disagreed with the report's recommendation but stated it is actively pursuing a two-phased process for assessing and prioritizing privacy-related initiatives.

audience.text: This report is for the Chairman, Subcommittee on Oversight of Government Management, the Federal Workforce, and the District of Columbia, Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, U.S. Senate, to inform oversight of HHS's efforts to ensure privacy in health information technology.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This is a GAO report (GAO-08-180) on the significant limitations of first responders' ability to detect and model hazardous releases in urban areas. It covers limitations in CBRN detection equipment, performance standards and testing, plume models for urban dispersion, and data gaps on urban population effects.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report finds that more than 6 years after September 11, 2001, local first responders do not have tools that can accurately and quickly identify CBRN releases in urban environments. Key findings include: radiological detection equipment cannot predict atmospheric dispersion; chemical detectors are inadequate for harmful but sublethal levels; handheld biological detectors are unreliable; BioWatch does not provide real-time detection; DHS has adopted only four CBRN detection equipment standards (none for chemical or biological); DHS does not independently test manufacturers' claims; nonurban and urban plume models have significant limitations for urban settings; and significant data gaps exist on effects of CBRN releases on urban populations.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The report states: 22 persons contracted anthrax disease and 5 died in the 2001 anthrax attacks; 6,000 people killed and $300 million economic damages in a sarin scenario; as of October 30, 2007, DHS had adopted 39 total standards for CBRN equipment but only 4 for radiation detection and none for chemical or biological detection; 800,000 shipments of hazardous materials travel daily; 3,800 killed in Bhopal; 11,500 gallons of chlorine released in Graniteville, 9 died, 529 sought medical care, 5,453 evacuated; BioWatch spending fiscal years 2005 to 2007 was about $236 million; approximately $3.2 million of SHSP and UASI grant funds in 2004-2005 in Washington, about $500,000 in Seattle, about $1.8 million in Connecticut in 2003-2005; IMS and SAW sensitivity for nerve agents is approximately 2 ppb to 20 ppb, limit of detection for blister agents 200 ppb to 300 ppb; CAMEO/ALOHA does not make predictions beyond 6.2 miles (10 kilometers) or more than an hour; NARAC/IMAAC can provide automated prediction within 5 to 15 minutes; 1,127 certifications and 268 operational suitability testing reports in RKB as of October 2007; 29 modeling systems evaluated in August 2002; more than 140 documented modeling systems; National Building Statistics Database contains data for 17 U.S. cities at 250-meter grid cell resolution and high-rise footprints for 46 cities; LandScan 2006 developed a high-resolution daytime population database; 75 cities in the continental United States with databases added by DOD; standards take 3 to 5 years; standards for radiation detection developed in 12 to 18 months.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends that the Secretary of Homeland Security: (1) reach agreement with other agencies on which agency should have the mission and responsibility to develop, test, and certify detection equipment for first responders' use in detecting hazardous material releases in the atmosphere; (2) ensure that manufacturers' claims are independently tested and validated regarding whether commercial off-the-shelf CBRN detection equipment can detect given hazardous material at specific sensitivities; (3) refine IMAAC's procedures by working with other federal, state, and local agencies to develop common/joint IMAAC emergency response practices, refine the concept of operations for chemical, biological, and radiological releases, and delineate the type and scale of major CBRN incidents that would qualify for IMAAC assistance; and (4) in conjunction with IMAAC, work with the federal plume modeling community to accelerate research and development to address plume model deficiencies in urban areas, including improvements to meteorological information, plume models, and data sets to evaluate plume models.

Dose response parameters for the general population do not exist for most chemical warfare agents. The report notes that DHS concurred with recommendations but stated GAO should consider other scenarios; DOC stated plume models would still have limitations even with implementation of recommendations.

about.text: This GAO report examines the status of undisbursed grant balances in expired grant accounts within the federal Payment Management System (PMS), focusing on the amount of undisbursed funds, common program characteristics, causes of grant closeout problems, and actions taken by federal agencies to improve closeout processes.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The document finds that during calendar year 2006, about $1 billion in undisbursed funding remained in expired grant accounts in PMS, representing about 1 percent of total funds made available for all expired grant accounts. For expired accounts with remaining undisbursed balances, the undisbursed funding represented, on average, about 26 percent of the original funding made available in 2006. These accounts were associated with thousands of grantees in over 325 different federal grant programs. Audit reports and Performance and Accountability Reports indicate undisbursed balances have been a long-standing challenge, attributed to low management priority, inconsistent procedures, poorly timed communications, and insufficient enforcement. Agencies such as HHS, DOJ, and EPA improved closeout timeliness and reduced balances when they made concerted efforts.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: About $1 billion in undisbursed funding in expired grant accounts during 2006; about 70 percent of federal grant disbursements handled by PMS in 2006; about 1 percent of total funds made available for all expired grant accounts during 2006; about 26 percent average undisbursed funding for accounts with undisbursed balances in 2006; over 325 different federal grant programs; $300 billion in federal grant awards in 2000; over $450 billion in 2006; about one-sixth of the federal budget in grants; 4 calendar years of data (2003-2006); 15 of 16 quarters with at least four departments having over 100 expired accounts; funding awards from over $100,000 to $100 million; 37 percent of EPA grants closed within 180 days in fiscal year 2005; $172 million in undisbursed funding that could have been deobligated per DOJ OIG; 11,356 to 6,237 OJP backlog reduction from 2001 to 2005; 180 days to 120 days timeline shortening; 10 days reduction in response time; 4,136 grants closed in Operation Closeout; over $30 million in deobligated funds; 64,000 HHS grants with remaining balance of $1.6 billion; 75 percent of these grants expired for more than 2 years; 90 percent EPA closure goal; 95 percent closure rate; over 150 audit reports reviewed; 2000 to 2006 period for audit reports; 13 funding ranges; 328 unique grant programs with positive undisbursed balances; 54 formula-based; 274 project-based; 26 grant programs with no time limit excluded; over 200,000 open grants in PMS as of June 2007; over $1.3 trillion total funding for open grants as of May 2007; over $320 billion in payments processed in 2006.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document recommends that the Director of OMB instruct all executive departments and independent agencies to: (1) annually track the amount of undisbursed grant funding remaining in expired grant accounts; and (2) report on the status and resolution of the undisbursed funding in their annual performance plan and in their annual Performance and Accountability Report, including the amount of undisbursed grant funding, why these funds were undisbursed, actions taken to resolve the undisbursed funding and close expired grants and related accounts, and outcomes associated with these actions.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that the results for program characteristics could not be compared to all closed federal grants or all closed grants using PMS due to the burden of collecting comparable data. It also notes that it cannot know whether the program characteristics represent a disproportionate share without comparative data. Additionally, the independent analysis of each program characteristic cannot be combined into a general statement, and the document did not interview policy experts or agency grant managers to explore why different characteristics might have larger undisbursed balances. OMB did not commit to implementing the recommendations and did not favor requiring agencies to report these balances in their PARs.

about.text: This GAO report (GAO-08-525) examines federal agency efforts to encrypt sensitive information, covering commercially available encryption technologies, relevant federal laws, policies, and guidance, and the extent to which 24 major federal agencies have implemented or planned encryption. It also reports on weaknesses in encryption practices at six selected agencies and makes recommendations to OMB and six agencies.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The document's findings include: (1) many commercially available encryption technologies can help agencies protect sensitive information and reduce risks, but incorrect implementation can create false security or render data inaccessible; (2) federal laws like FISMA, the Privacy Act, and HIPAA provide a framework, while OMB memorandums (M-06-16 and M-07-16) recommend and require encryption of mobile devices; (3) all 24 agencies had initiated encryption efforts, but stored data encryption lagged behind transmission encryption—about 70% of laptops and handhelds were not encrypted; (4) none of the agencies had documented comprehensive implementation plans; (5) weaknesses existed at six selected agencies in installation, configuration, monitoring, policies, and training; and (6) risks from data breaches, such as the 2006 VA incident, underscore the need for improved encryption practices.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: Figures cited in the document include: 26.5 million veterans and military personnel affected by the 2006 VA data breach; 4,000 participants in a Defense laptop theft (February 2008); 100,000 archived employment records in a TSA external drive loss (May 2007); 3,634 incidents reported to US-CERT in FY2005, 5,503 in FY2006, and 13,029 in FY2007 (about 259% increase); 10 of 24 agencies reported encrypting less than 20% of laptops/handhelds, 5 reported 20-39%, 2 reported 40-59%, 3 reported 60-79%, and 6 reported 80-100%; about 70% of laptops and handhelds not encrypted; 10 of 22 agencies reported encrypting less than 20% of portable storage media offsite; 3 of 22 reported 20-39%; 9 of 17 agencies reported encrypting less than 20% of offsite backup storage; for wired Internet transmissions, 18 of 23 agencies reported 80-100% encryption; for wireless transmissions, 12 of 21 reported 80-100%; 18 of 24 agencies had not completed inventorying sensitive information; at selected agencies, 2 of 6 had not installed FIPS-validated modules, 4 had not configured properly, all 6 lacked documented policies/procedures, and 3 had not adequately trained personnel; HUD had no encryption on any laptops; Education had no FIPS-validated product on 15 tested laptops; USDA, State, GSA had installed on all 58 tested laptops; NASA had installed on 27 of 29 tested laptops; USDA had not monitored 5 of 52 laptops; 3 of 6 agencies had not configured BlackBerry devices; Education had one of three VPNs non-FIPS-compliant; 20 recommendations made.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document recommends that the Director of OMB take two actions: (1) clarify governmentwide policy requiring agencies to encrypt sensitive agency data through additional guidance and/or educational activities; (2) monitor the effectiveness of agencies' encryption implementation plans and efforts to inventory sensitive information. It also makes 18 recommendations to six agencies: USDA (3 actions), Department of Education (5 actions), HUD (3 actions), Department of State (2 actions), GSA (2 actions), and NASA (3 actions)—covering installing/configuring FIPS-compliant products, developing policies/procedures for key management, monitoring installation/functioning, and providing training. These are the actions the document calls for.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that none of the 24 agencies had documented comprehensive encryption implementation plans, and 18 had not completed inventorying sensitive information. It notes uncertainty among agencies regarding the applicability of OMB's encryption requirements, as OMB's description of 'mobile computers and devices' was not clear in its memorandums. It also identifies limits in OMB's monitoring, as OMB did not provide evidence of monitoring inventories or plans. The document notes that agencies like HUD had delayed encryption due to funding, and that some agencies had not resolved issues like enabling content protection on BlackBerry devices or training personnel.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This is a GAO report assessing U.S. Customs and Border Protection's efforts to develop and implement international supply chain security standards, achieve mutual recognition of customs security practices, and address challenges posed by the statutory requirement to scan 100 percent of U.S.-bound container cargo at foreign seaports.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: CBP has taken a lead role in developing and implementing international supply chain security standards, including the WCO SAFE Framework, and has worked to achieve mutual recognition of customs security practices with other countries. However, CBP and international partners report challenges in balancing these efforts with the statutory requirement to scan 100 percent of U.S.-bound container cargo, which could adversely impact implementation of international standards, may provide lower security, and could disproportionately affect trade with developing countries.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: 154 of 173 WCO member countries had signed letters of intent to implement the SAFE Framework as of June 2008. 11 million oceangoing cargo containers arrived at U.S. seaports in fiscal year 2007--roughly 30,000 each day. 58 foreign seaports participate in the CSI program. As of May 2008, there were over 8,400 C-TPAT members. As of April 2008, 111 countries were participating in the WCO capacity-building program; 104 had completed the first phase, 65 had moved into the second, and one was in the third as of July 2008. CBP provided training and assistance to 10 countries in the capacity-building program. About 70 countries have begun developing their own national AEO programs. In June 2007, CBP signed a mutual recognition arrangement with New Zealand--the first such arrangement in the world. CBP later signed mutual recognition arrangements with Jordan and Canada in June 2008. CBP and the European Commission agreed to establish mutual recognition of customs-to-business partnership programs by early 2009. The 9/11 Act requires 100 percent scanning of all U.S.-bound container cargo by 2012, with possible extensions.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document does not make recommendations; it is a GAO report that assesses CBP's efforts and notes challenges, but does not recommend specific actions.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document notes that the full impacts of the Secure Freight Initiative pilot program are still unknown, that it is unclear who will pay for the additional resources needed to implement the 100 percent scanning requirement, and that the results of seaport visits and perspectives of foreign officials cannot be generalized. It also notes that mutual recognition of customs controls presents a challenge and may not be easily or quickly attained.

audience.name: Who it is for
audience.text: The document is for congressional requesters, including specific Senate and House committees, and supports oversight and decision-making regarding CBP's international supply chain security efforts and the 100 percent scanning requirement.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report assesses the progress of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) in implementing recommendations from a 2003 report and other steps to improve monitoring and tracking of radioactive materials, and the ability of the Department of Homeland Security's Customs and Border Protection (CBP) to detect and verify the legitimacy of radioactive materials at U.S. ports of entry.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: NRC has implemented three of six recommendations from GAO's 2003 report, including identifying 16 radionuclides of concern, establishing increased controls for category 2 or greater quantities, and developing performance criteria. NRC has made limited progress on other recommendations, such as fixing licensing vulnerabilities that allowed GAO investigators to obtain a license using a fictitious business. NRC's new tracking systems (National Source Tracking System and Web-based licensing system) have been delayed; the NSTS is expected to launch January 2009 and the Web-based system in summer 2010. CBP has a comprehensive radiation detection system at borders, but personal radiation detectors are in short supply, and CBP's 2006 guidance on when to contact the National Targeting Center to verify licenses was not effectively communicated to officers, leading to some dangerous materials entering without verification.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: About 2 million sealed sources are licensed for use in the United States. Approximately 22,000 specific materials licenses exist; NRC administers about 3,750 and agreement states the rest. NRC has relinquished authority to 35 states. The NSTS has been delayed by 18 months; expansion to category 3 and largest category 4 sources is expected by at least March 2010. CBP needs about 1,500 personal radiation detectors for current officers and about 2,000 more for new hires, a total shortfall of about 3,500. Over 90 percent of personally owned vehicles at land ports pass through radiation portal monitors. NRC has performed preliminary increased controls inspections on approximately 1,100 of 1,700 licensees. The interim database includes information from 99 percent of all licensees. Agreement states represent over 80 percent of all U.S. licenses for these materials.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document recommends that the Chairman of the NRC ensure priority attention to meeting the January 2009 and summer 2010 target dates for launching the National Source Tracking System, Web-based licensing system, and the new license verification system, and complete steps to include all potentially dangerous radioactive sources in the NSTS as quickly as possible. It recommends that the Secretary of Homeland Security direct the Commissioner of CBP to effectively communicate current CBP guidance to officers at ports of entry regarding when to contact the National Targeting Center to verify legitimacy of radioactive materials, and to take measures to ensure this guidance is followed.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document notes that NRC has not yet determined how to effectively mitigate potential psychological effects of an RDD, has not decided whether certain radioactive sources need stronger licensing requirements (rulemaking process initiated in September 2007, estimated to take about 2 years), and that delays in the NSTS and Web-based licensing system may lead to further postponements. CBP's review of its 2003 radiation detection program directive was delayed pending resolution of unrelated matters.

audience.text: The report is addressed to the Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, U.S. Senate.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report examines the magnitude of unpaid federal payroll taxes owed by businesses, the factors affecting IRS's ability to enforce compliance and collect these taxes, and evidence of abusive or potentially criminal activity by some businesses. It is a report to Congressional Committees, based on an audit conducted from April 2007 through May 2008.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report finds that as of September 30, 2007, over 1.6 million businesses owed over $58 billion in unpaid payroll taxes, including interest and penalties. IRS's collection approach focuses primarily on voluntary compliance, which can allow egregious offenders to accumulate debt for years. IRS is not timely filing liens or assessing Trust Fund Recovery Penalties, and does not treat the business's payroll tax debt and responsible party's penalty as a single collection effort. IRS lacks performance measures for payroll tax collection. Some businesses engaged in abusive or potentially criminal activity, such as diverting withheld taxes for personal use. The report also notes that states use tools like publishing tax debtor names and matching bank accounts to identify levy sources, which IRS is prohibited from or has not implemented.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: As of September 30, 2007: over 1.6 million businesses owed over $58 billion in unpaid payroll taxes. 70 percent of unpaid payroll taxes owed by businesses with more than a year (4 tax quarters) of unpaid taxes; over a quarter owed by businesses with more than 3 years (12 quarters). The General Fund transferred $44 billion to trust funds over what IRS collected as of November 1, 2007. 52 percent ($30 billion) of unpaid payroll taxes classified as currently uncollectible; $7 billion assigned to revenue officers; $9 billion in queue. Over 14,000 businesses owed payroll taxes for 20 or more quarters (5 years), up from 5,367 in 1998; 490 businesses owed for over 40 quarters (10 years), up from 86. IRS took over 40 weeks to decide TFRP and additional 40 weeks to assess. In fiscal year 2007, IRS collected over $17 billion from almost 3 million tax debtors through installment agreements; filed more than 680,000 tax liens; over 3.7 million levy actions; 676 seizure actions. IRS obtained less than 10 injunctions in fiscal year 2007. Over 1,500 individuals responsible for non-payment at 3 or more businesses; 18 responsible for 12 different businesses. In fiscal year 2007, IRS processed over 230 million tax returns and collected over $2.7 trillion in taxes. IRS estimates the annual net tax gap at nearly $300 billion. The 76-case sample showed average time to assess TFRP was over 2 years from business tax debt assessment. For over a third of businesses with unpaid payroll taxes assigned to field, IRS had not filed a lien; over 80 percent of cases in queue did not have a lien. In a 2005 IRS study, less than half of TFRP cases had a lien filed; only 8 percent of TFRP assessments (over $11.9 billion between 1996 and 2004) were collected. Half of TFRP assessments not assigned to a revenue officer; over half of those assigned were not assigned to the same officer working the business case.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report makes six recommendations to the Commissioner of IRS. Five recommendations are for IRS to review or revise its collection policies to provide better monitoring or more detailed guidance on collection actions against egregious payroll tax offenders and to strengthen existing collection tools. The sixth recommendation is for IRS to work with states to develop ways of more effectively identifying potential levy sources. IRS concurred with all six recommendations.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report notes that IRS's estimate of the tax gap and unpaid taxes understates the true cumulative amount because many tax debts go unidentified or unrecorded. It also states that the estimate of $44 billion transferred to trust funds does not include tax debts written off in previous years due to expiration of the statutory collection period. The report notes that IRS was unable to determine how many seizure actions in fiscal year 2007 were taken against payroll tax debtors. It also notes that the number of repeat offenders identified (1,500 and 18) represents only those assessed TFRPs and not the total number of repeat offenders. The report acknowledges that IRS's traditional collection methods do not always bring taxpayers into compliance and that there remains a major compliance problem.

audience.name: Who it is for
audience.text: This report is intended for Congressional Committees, to inform them about the magnitude of unpaid payroll taxes and the effectiveness of IRS's collection efforts.

about.text: This document is a GAO report to the Subcommittee on Investigations and Oversight of the House Committee on Science and Technology on the Department of Energy's Office of Science project management. It evaluates the extent to which the Office of Science managed its projects within committed cost and schedule targets from fiscal year 2003 through fiscal year 2007, identifies key factors affecting performance, and outlines main challenges for the future.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The document reports that of 42 projects reviewed, more than two-thirds were completed or carried out within original cost and schedule targets. Specifically, of 27 completed projects, 24 (89 percent) met original cost targets and 21 (78 percent) were completed on or ahead of schedule. Of 15 ongoing projects, 9 were on track to meet both targets. Factors contributing to performance include leadership commitment, management and technical expertise, disciplined oversight, and occasional scope trimming. Future challenges include funding uncertainties and workforce retirements.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The document states that of 27 completed projects, 24 (89 percent) met original cost targets and 21 (78 percent) were on schedule. Of 15 ongoing projects, 9 (60 percent) were on track for both targets. 5 of 27 completed projects (19 percent) met one target but not both, and 2 (7 percent) were both over budget and late. For ongoing projects, 4 (27 percent) expected to meet cost but not schedule, and 2 (13 percent) expected to miss both. Specific examples: Run IIb CDF Detector completed for about $10.9 million versus $30.4 million target, 4 months ahead of schedule; Center for Nanoscale Materials completed on schedule within $72 million cost; Neutrinos at the Main Injector completed 17 months late and over 23 percent over its $168 million committed cost; Stanford Positron-Electron Asymmetric Ring (SPEAR 3 Upgrade) completed 14 months late and nearly 18 percent over its $49 million target; National Compact Stellarator Experiment facing cost increase of 91 percent and 4.5-year delay; Large Area Telescope costs increased from $121 million to $188 million, with DOE contribution rising from $37 million to $45 million; International Thermonuclear Energy Reactor received $10.7 million instead of $160 million requested for fiscal year 2008; Office of Science workforce eligible for retirement expected to increase from 21 percent in 2005 to 43 percent by 2011.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document recommends that the Secretary of Energy direct the Director of the Office of Engineering and Construction Management to consider whether other DOE program offices would benefit from adopting selected practices from the Office of Science's independent project reviews, such as the frequency and focus of reviews for technically complex projects. It also recommends that the Office of Engineering and Construction Management review and strengthen DOE's project management guidance to help ensure each project's technical goals, including expected scientific performance and facility requirements, are clearly and sufficiently defined.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that the nongeneralizable sample of 12 projects selected for in-depth review cannot be used to make inferences about overall performance. It notes that concerns about scope reductions were raised by DOE's Office of Engineering and Construction Management and its Inspector General, and that there is disagreement over the effect of scope changes on technical goals for the Spallation Neutron Source. The document also notes that DOE's Office of Engineering and Construction Management is considering clarifying project management guidance on defining technical goals, perhaps by 2009. Additionally, it notes that contractor laboratories had not yet estimated the shortfall in project management and scientific expertise due to retirements.

audience.name: Who it is for
audience.text: This report is intended for the Subcommittee on Investigations and Oversight of the House Committee on Science and Technology to inform congressional oversight of DOE's Office of Science project management.

about.text: This document is a GAO report (GAO-08-642R) to congressional subcommittees on the Department of Energy's management of costs and liabilities for contractors' pension and postretirement benefit plans, covering DOE's analysis supporting its April 2006 Notice 351.1 policy changes, the distribution of liabilities, and recent actions to manage future costs.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The document's own findings include that DOE recognized historical and possible future trends of liabilities, but the documentation DOE provided contained only limited evidence that DOE considered policy alternatives, stakeholder sensitivities, or near- and long-term financial and mission impacts of the changes; that the decision document for Notice 351.1 did not include the basis for approval; that as of September 30, 2007, the net funded status (net liability) was $69.5 million for pension plans and $10.3 billion for postretirement plans; and that since 2005, DOE has awarded 14 contracts with new provisions limiting pension and postretirement benefits for new employees to no more than 105 percent of comparable organizations.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: In 2007, contractors contributed $387 million and $334 million to defined benefit pension and postretirement plans; DOE reported a net liability of $69.5 million for defined benefit pensions and $10.3 billion for postretirement benefits; as of September 30, 2007, benefit obligations were approximately $27.5 billion (pension) and $10.5 billion (postretirement), with assets of $27.4 billion and $161.6 million; from fiscal years 1997 to 2007, the net funded status of postretirement benefits declined from an underfunding of $5.0 billion to $10.3 billion; pension underfunding changed from $4.5 billion in fiscal year 2006 to $69.5 million in fiscal year 2007. The table for fiscal year 2007 shows total pension benefit obligations of ($27,512.9) million, assets of $27,443.4 million, and net funded status of ($69.5) million; postretirement benefit obligations of ($10,318.6) million, assets of $161.6 million, and net funded status of ($10,480.2) million.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document does not recommend any actions; it reports on DOE's actions and policies. Under DOE Order 350.1, if a contractor's total benefit value or cost study score exceeds 105 percent of its comparison group, DOE may require a corrective action plan. about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report examines the extent to which federal benefit programs use electronic payment methods to disburse benefits, identifies factors agencies consider when implementing or using electronic payments, and identifies potential options for increasing their use, particularly Treasury's actions. It is based on a survey of 42 federal benefit programs and interviews with agencies, industry representatives, and consumer groups.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: Most federal benefit programs surveyed (34 of 42) used one or more electronic payment methods. Direct deposit was the most common method, and the majority of these programs said most of their recipients received benefits electronically. However, data limitations prevented determining the extent of electronic payment use for most agencies. Six programs did not use electronic payments and disbursed benefits by paper check. Agencies consider factors such as financial burden to recipients, program and recipient characteristics, program costs, and fraud and security risks when deciding on electronic payment methods. Options to increase use include new statutory requirements, public outreach, adapting payment cards, and Treasury initiatives like the Go Direct campaign and the Direct Express debit card.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: For 18 programs that provided data, the percentage of payments made electronically ranged from about 5 to 100 percent; for the 5 largest of these, about 54 to 100 percent were made electronically. 8 of the 18 programs paid 100 percent of benefit payments electronically, but 6 of these were education assistance programs. 13 programs provided data on paper check payments; 9 distributed less than half of the total dollar value by paper check, and 4 distributed 100 percent by paper check. In fiscal year 2006, the Social Security Retirement Insurance program distributed $418 billion in benefit payments, the largest surveyed. Treasury disbursed 81.6 percent of benefits electronically as of fiscal year 2008 (through January), compared to 56 percent in fiscal year 1996. In 2006, electronic payments numbered 62.7 billion with a value of $34.1 trillion, while checks numbered 30.6 billion with a value of $41.7 trillion.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends that the Secretary of the Treasury direct the Commissioner of FMS to consider developing a process for conducting outreach to federal agencies on a more regular basis, with the goal of identifying opportunities for increasing the use of electronic payments. For example, Treasury could meet with agency CFOs or their designees and staff from smaller agencies on a semiannual or annual basis to discuss challenges and identify actions to facilitate the transition to electronic payments.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report notes data limitations prevented determining the extent to which most agencies used electronic payments, in part because states are responsible for disbursing payments for many federal benefit programs and are not required to provide specific payment data. The report also states that the most-sweeping option to increase electronic payment use—mandating electronic payments—would present challenges, though they could be overcome. Additionally, Treasury has no plans to conduct outreach to CFO agencies and other smaller agencies on a regular basis, according to the report.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report examines the status of property conveyances and transfers between the District of Columbia and the federal government as directed by Public Law 109-396, including progress on development of the exchanged properties and challenges going forward.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: As of June 6, 2008, no property conveyances had occurred, although all transfers of administrative jurisdiction became effective on December 15, 2006. The report identifies that several factors have slowed the conveyances, including negotiations about cleanup, testing for contamination, disagreement over land to be conveyed as part of the Boathouse Row properties, and decision changes about environmental impact statement development for Poplar Point. Limited development has occurred on the properties, and development of the largest properties, Poplar Point and Reservation 13, will likely take up to a decade. The District and federal government face challenges including cleanup uncertainties, relocating U.S. Park Police facilities, transitioning the Deputy Mayor's Office to a development coordination role, and reaching community agreement on development.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The report states that the District's structural fiscal imbalance likely exceeded $470 million annually and could have been as high as $1.1 billion. Poplar Point is a 110-acre property; Reservation 13 is 67 acres. The Master Developer's vision for Poplar Point includes 1.5 million square feet of office space, 3.8 million square feet of residential units, 405,000 square feet of retail space, and 70 acres of parks. Reservation 13 is planned to accommodate about 3,000 new housing units, nearly 5.5 million square feet of mixed-use development, and more than $80 million in new infrastructure upgrades. NPS facilities at Poplar Point encompass 100,000 square feet and sit on approximately 18 acres. DMPED staff increased from 33 FTEs in September 2007 to 63 FTEs in June 2008, expected to grow to 73 by August 2008.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report makes no explicit recommendations. It notes that the District must complete several steps to meet conditions in Public Law 109-396, including developing a Secretary of the Interior-approved land-use plan for Poplar Point, and that the NPS Director must certify replacement facilities are ready for occupancy before conveyance of NPS facilities. It also notes that the District and GSA must agree on a property of not more than 12 acres to convey to the AOC.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report notes that cleanup and development uncertainties at Poplar Point, including the extent and location of cleanup, cost, responsibility for payment, potential complications of relocating USPP facilities, and the amount of construction allowed prior to certification, are unresolved. The definition of 'construction project' under the statute is unclear. The date for completion of conveyances between the District and GSA is uncertain, depending on agreement for the AOC site. The exact boundaries of the Boathouse Row property have not been resolved.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a GAO report on the Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) and the Health Center Program. It examines the extent to which medically underserved areas (MUAs) lacked health center sites in 2006 and 2007, the types of services provided at those sites, and HRSA's oversight of cooperative agreement recipients and feedback to unsuccessful grant applicants.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The document's findings include: In 2006, 47 percent of MUAs nationwide lacked a health center site; the percentage varied widely by region and state. New access point awards in 2007 reduced the number of MUAs lacking a site by about 7 percent, leaving 43 percent lacking a site in 2007. HRSA does not collect data on services provided at individual health center sites, so the extent of access to comprehensive primary care services in MUAs is unknown. HRSA's oversight of training and technical assistance cooperative agreement recipients is limited because it lacks standardized performance measures and is unlikely to meet its policy timeline for on-site reviews. Additionally, 38 percent of summary statements sent to unsuccessful applicants contained unclear feedback.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: In 2006, 47 percent of MUAs nationwide lacked a health center site; this was 1,600 of 3,421 MUAs. In 2007, 43 percent of MUAs lacked a site, which was 1,487 MUAs. The 2007 awards reduced the number by about 7 percent, or 113 fewer MUAs. In 2006, 32 percent of all MUAs contained more than one health center site; among MUAs with at least one site, 60 percent contained multiple sites. In 2007, 202 new access point grants were awarded; the South census region received 101 (50 percent), the West received 47 (23 percent), the Midwest received 39 (19 percent), and the Northeast received 15 (7 percent). In the 2007 High Poverty County competition, 69 percent of awards went to the South; in the open competition, the South received 49 awards (39 percent), the West 45 (35 percent), the Midwest 21 (17 percent), and the Northeast 12 (9 percent). For fiscal years 2005 and 2007, 38 percent of summary statements contained unclear feedback, 13 percent in more than one criterion, and there were 41 distinct examples of unclear feedback. HRSA had evaluated only about 20 percent of cooperative agreement recipients since 2004. HRSA awarded nearly $53 million in cooperative agreements for fiscal year 2007.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document recommends that the Administrator of HRSA take four actions: collect and maintain readily available data on the types of services provided at each health center site; develop and implement standardized performance measures for training and technical assistance cooperative agreement recipients, including a measure of the number of successful applicants assisted; reevaluate the policy of conducting comprehensive on-site reviews every 3 to 5 years and consider targeting resources to recipients most likely to benefit; and identify and take appropriate action to ensure that the discussion of strengths and weaknesses in all summary statements is clear.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document does not settle the following: HRSA does not collect data on services provided at individual health center sites, so the extent of access to comprehensive primary care services in MUAs is unknown. HRSA's oversight is limited because it lacks standardized performance measures, and it is unlikely to meet its policy timeline for comprehensive on-site reviews. The document also notes that the new access point awards in 2007 had little impact on the wide geographic variation in the percentage of MUAs lacking a health center site. HHS raised concerns about the exclusion of MUPs from the analysis, which the report states were beyond the scope of the work.

about.text: This is a GAO report on the Republic of Palau's use of and accountability for U.S. assistance provided under the Compact of Free Association, and on Palau's prospects for economic self-sufficiency. It covers U.S. assistance from 1995 through 2009, accountability efforts from 1995 through 2006, and factors affecting Palau's economic self-sufficiency.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: Key findings: U.S. assistance to Palau in 1995-2009 is projected to exceed $852 million, with compact direct assistance accounting for $411 million, federal services about $25 million, road construction $149 million, and discretionary programs about $267 million. Palau made progress in financial accountability but has limited capacity to address persistent internal control weaknesses; Interior's oversight has been limited. Palau's prospects for economic self-sufficiency depend on levels of continued U.S. assistance, trust fund withdrawals, fiscal reform, and private sector growth.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This is a GAO report on how veteran students received similar amounts of Title IV federal student aid as nonveterans, but more total federal aid when Montgomery GI Bill Chapter 30 benefits were included, based on data from the 2005-2006 academic year for first-year full-time students.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The document's key findings are that overall, veteran students received similar amounts of Title IV aid as nonveteran, independent students, but when including Chapter 30 GI benefits, veterans received more total federal aid than nonveterans. Laws and regulations largely dictate how schools allocate Title IV aid, but five of the eight schools interviewed used their limited flexibility to allow veterans to be eligible for larger amounts of certain types of Title IV aid. While federal agencies and schools provide the same information on Title IV aid to all students, two of the schools interviewed in areas with nearby military bases reach out to veteran students, and in 2007 Education began new efforts to inform veterans about Title IV aid.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: In fiscal year 2007, the Department of Education provided $82 billion in financial aid under Title IV to 11 million students. VA awarded about $2 billion in Chapter 30 education benefits to more than 300,000 veteran students in fiscal year 2007. In academic year 2005 to 2006, veterans received on average $2,322 in Pell Grants, $2,082 in subsidized Stafford Loans, $2,959 in unsubsidized Stafford Loans, and $1,450 in campus-based aid (2003-2004 estimate), while nonveterans received $2,482, $2,109, $2,945, and $1,300 respectively. Veterans received an average of $9,306 in Chapter 30 GI benefits. Veterans received on average 6 percent less in Pell Grants than nonveterans. At the 75th percentile in income at public 2-year schools, veterans earned an average of $38,550 the year before starting school, compared to $33,259 for nonveterans; veterans were eligible for a Pell Grant of $1,600, compared to $2,100 for nonveterans. Chapter 30 GI benefit rate was $1,034 per month in academic year 2005 to 2006.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document does not make explicit recommendations, but notes that the report does not address how reservists' federal financial aid compares with other students, and states this may warrant further inquiry given the increasing number of reservists called to active duty and differences in their GI benefits.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that its scope did not include reservists, who can receive benefits under other GI Bill chapters. It also notes that the report does not address how the federal financial aid amounts reservists receive compare with other students, which may warrant further inquiry. The document mentions that the numbers for campus-based aid were not significantly different at the 95 percent confidence level, and that findings from the eight schools interviewed cannot be generalized beyond those schools.
