about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report assesses the Department of Defense's implementation of the National Security Personnel System (NSPS), focusing on the extent to which internal safeguards ensure fairness, effectiveness, and credibility, and on DOD civilian employee perceptions of NSPS. It is a report to congressional committees based on a GAO audit conducted from August 2007 to July 2008.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The document's findings are that while DOD has taken steps to implement internal safeguards for NSPS, implementation of three safeguards could be improved: predecisional internal safeguards, reasonable transparency, and meaningful distinctions in employee performance. Specifically, DOD does not require a third-party predecisional analysis of rating results for anomalies; some installations do not publish final rating distributions; and guidance may discourage using all rating categories. The document also finds that NSPS employees are more positive than other DOD employees about some performance management aspects, but attitudes among those with the most experience under NSPS have declined. DOD does not have an action plan to address generally negative employee perceptions. The document makes four recommendations to the Secretary of Defense.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: Key figures include: over 182,000 DOD civilian employees phased into NSPS as of May 2008 (total 182,630); approximately 273,000 employees remaining to be phased in; the estimated cost to implement NSPS from fiscal years 2009 through 2011 is approximately $143 million; in the May 2007 survey, an estimated 43 percent of NSPS employees and 25 percent of all other DOD employees agreed that pay raises depend on how well employees perform their jobs; the estimated percentage of spiral 1.1 employees who agreed that their performance appraisal was a fair reflection of performance declined from 67 percent in May 2006 to 52 percent in May 2007; the percentage who believed NSPS would have a positive effect on DOD's personnel practices dropped from 40 percent in May 2006 to 23 percent in May 2007; DOD-wide rating distribution as of the report was 0.2% at rating 1, 1.6% at rating 2, 57.0% at rating 3, 36.1% at rating 4, and 5.1% at rating 5; at least one installation had 84% of employees rated at category 3 (Marine Corps Tactical Systems Support Activity). DOD received over 58,000 comments on proposed NSPS rules; a survey of employees for performance factors received responses from approximately 14% (71,000 employees).

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document recommends that the Secretary of Defense direct the NSPS Senior Executive to take four actions: (1) require a third party to perform predecisional demographic and other analysis as appropriate for pay pools; (2) require commands to publish the final overall rating results; (3) provide guidance to pay pools and supervisors that encourages them to rate employees appropriately, including using all categories of ratings as warranted; and (4) develop and implement a specific action plan to address employee perceptions of NSPS ascertained from feedback avenues such as DOD's survey and DOD's and GAO's employee focus groups.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document notes several unsettled points: DOD did not concur with the recommendation to require a third-party predecisional analysis, arguing that postdecisional analysis is more useful; GAO continued to believe the recommendation has merit. DOD partially concurred with the recommendations to encourage use of all rating categories and to develop an action plan, noting it will address areas of weakness. The document also states that the overall trend in employee attitudes is not known, and that it will be possible to identify trends after more surveys are administered. The information from GAO discussion groups is not generalizable to the entire DOD civilian population. DOD has not developed a new timeline for phasing in the remaining approximately 273,000 employees.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a GAO report (GAO-08-823) on the roles, capabilities, and challenges of major national voluntary organizations in providing mass care and other human services in large-scale disasters. It examines four main questions: the roles of these organizations, steps taken since Hurricane Katrina to strengthen capacity, known current capabilities, and remaining challenges. The report focuses on the American Red Cross, The Salvation Army, the Southern Baptist Convention, Catholic Charities USA, and the United Way, and includes site visits to Los Angeles, Miami, New York City, and Washington D.C. It also discusses FEMA's coordination with these organizations and makes recommendations to FEMA.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report finds that the voluntary organizations in the review are a major source of mass care and other services in large-scale disasters, with roles varying from direct service provision (Red Cross, Salvation Army, Southern Baptist Convention, Catholic Charities) to fund-raising (United Way). Four of the organizations have taken steps since Katrina to expand service coverage (e.g., Red Cross chapter reorganization, community partnerships) and strengthen coordination, logistics, and communications. The report also finds that initial assessments have not fully captured collective capabilities, and that a worst-case large-scale disaster would likely overwhelm voluntary organizations' current sheltering and feeding capabilities without government and other assistance. Key findings include: (1) the Red Cross's role in the National Response Framework changed from primary to support agency for mass care (ESF-6), but the Catastrophic Incident Supplement still describes it as primary, and there is no interim agreement documenting the changed role; (2) FEMA's 2007 survey of disaster capabilities assesses sheltering but not feeding, and does not include all voluntary organization capabilities; (3) except for the Red Cross, the other voluntary organizations have not assessed their own nationwide capabilities; (4) shortages of trained personnel, difficulty dedicating financial resources for preparedness, and coordination with government remain challenges.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The report states that after the 2005 hurricanes, the Red Cross raised more than $2.1 billion; The Salvation Army, $325 million; Catholic Charities USA, $150 million; the United Way, $28 million; and the Southern Baptist Convention, about $20 million. During Hurricane Katrina, the Red Cross provided more than 52.6 million meals and snacks, opened more than 1,300 shelters across 27 states, and had 245,000 volunteers. The Salvation Army provided 3.8 million articles of clothing, 7.7 million meals and snacks, 91,400 lodging spaces, and 506,443 volunteer hours. The Southern Baptist Convention provided 14.6 million meals and had 165,748 volunteer days. Catholic Charities USA provided 51 million pounds of food, and more than 110 dioceses responded. The Red Cross has a national headquarters and service area staff of about 1,600 as of May 2008, and a cadre of over 71,000 volunteers who are nationally deployable. The Red Cross reported a projected operating budget deficit for fiscal year 2008 of about $150 million. In early 2008, the Red Cross reduced its staff by about 1,000; it reduced staff supporting state emergency management agencies from 14 to 5. The Red Cross requested $7 million annually for ESF-6 staffing and $3 million for integrating nongovernmental sector mass care services, for a total of $10 million. The Red Cross has identified 50,000 potential shelter facilities and enough sheltering supplies to support up to 500,000 people. In Los Angeles, Red Cross officials said local sheltering capacity is 84,000 people under optimal conditions. In a major earthquake in a metropolitan area, DHS estimates shelter for as many as 300,000 people. The report includes estimates of mass care needs: DHS Target Capabilities List (Sept 2007): sheltering 313,000 people, feeding 1.5 million meals per day for a 7.2-magnitude earthquake with a subsequent 8.0 earthquake in a major metropolitan area with approximately 10 million people; American Red Cross Risk-Based Capacity Building Initiative (July 2007): sheltering estimates of 564,113 for Southern California, 300,000 for Washington D.C., 605,000 for New York City metro area, 328,646 for Gulf Coast; feeding estimates of 2.5 million people will need feeding (Southern California), 4 million people will need feeding (New York City), 657,292 meals per day (Gulf Coast); Florida Division of Emergency Management Hurricane Ono planning project (Nov 2007): sheltering 885,000, feeding 3 million meals per day for a Category V hurricane in South Florida. As of June 2007, 2-1-1 coverage serves approximately 198 million Americans, or about 65 percent of the United States population, according to the United Way.

about.text: This GAO report assesses the Department of Homeland Security's (DHS) risk-based methodology for allocating Homeland Security Grant Program (HSGP) funds under the State Homeland Security Program (SHSP) and Urban Areas Security Initiative (UASI), focusing on changes from fiscal year 2007 to 2008 and the reasonableness of the fiscal year 2008 methodology.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: Key findings include: DHS's fiscal year 2008 methodology is primarily the same as fiscal year 2007, with the principal change being the use of Metropolitan Statistical Areas (MSAs) to define urban area boundaries. The risk analysis model is generally reasonable, but the vulnerability element has limitations because DHS assigned a constant vulnerability score of 1.0 to all states and urban areas, ignoring variations. The change to MSAs expanded eligible urban areas to 60 total UASI grantees. The model is robust for Tier 1 UASI areas but sensitivity for Tier 2 improved in fiscal year 2008 compared to 2007.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: Fiscal year 2007: approximately $1.7 billion distributed, $1.6 billion planned for fiscal year 2008. Since 2002, almost $20 billion distributed. $852 million allocated in fiscal year 2008 under the Infrastructure Protection Program. $410.8 million to 6 Tier 1 UASI grantees, $336.1 million to 39 Tier 2 UASI grantees in fiscal year 2007. $429.9 million to 7 Tier 1 UASI grantees, $351.7 million to 53 Tier 2 UASI grantees in fiscal year 2008. Fiscal year 2008 saw an increase of almost 162,000 square miles in total urban area footprints; other areas increased by almost 2,700 square miles on average. In fiscal year 2007, $410,795,000 was allocated to Tier 1, $336,105,000 to Tier 2; in fiscal year 2008, $429,896,500 to Tier 1, $351,733,500 to Tier 2. The statutory minimum for states was 0.375 percent of funds appropriated for SHSP and UASI in fiscal year 2008. The Threat Index accounted for 20 percent of the total risk score; the Vulnerability and Consequences Index accounted for 80 percent.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends that the Secretary of DHS instruct FEMA, I&A, and NPPD to formulate a method to measure vulnerability in a way that captures variations across states and urban areas, and apply this vulnerability measure in future iterations of the risk-based grant allocation model. The report states that FEMA and I&A concurred with this recommendation.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document notes that DHS did not measure vulnerability but assigned a constant value of 1.0, and that this ignores geographic differences. It also notes that DHS officials expressed limited confidence in the threat data, and that DHS did not provide details on criteria for the 'best fit' footprint choice. Additionally, the report notes that the analysis DHS used for peer review quality control did not apply a generally-accepted method to ensure inter-rater reliability, and DHS identified resource constraints as a reason for not measuring inter-rater reliability.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report, GAO-08-854, issued June 26, 2008, examines the extent to which federal agencies use the authorities of the Defense Production Act of 1950 (DPA) and assesses agencies' responses to reporting requirements on the economic impact of foreign offsets. It covers use of DPA authorities in defense, energy, domestic emergency and disaster response and recovery, and critical infrastructure, as well as foreign offsets issues.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The findings are GAO's own. Key findings include: DOD is the primary user of DPA Title I priorities and allocations authority, placing priority ratings on almost all of its contracts (approximately 300,000 annually), while civilian agencies generally have not used the authority and most would decide to place ratings case-by-case after a delivery issue arises. Civilian agencies responsible for civil transportation, health resources, and food and agriculture resources have not developed and implemented policies or guidance to use the Title I authority. DOD has generally been the sole user of Title III authority for expansion of production capabilities. Events triggering some Title VII authorities have not occurred. Efforts to assess foreign offsets have been limited; Commerce's data collection limits analysis of economic effects, and an interagency team has reached consensus with foreign nations that adverse effects exist but not on best practices. The National Commission on Offsets' final report was never produced.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The document states: 'approximately 300,000' contracts annually receive priority ratings under DPAS; DHS has authorized or endorsed the use of priority ratings 15 times since 2003; a less than 40 percent response rate to a survey of three tiers of subcontractors; 84 percent of the value of export contracts involving offsets submitted by prime contractors are for the aerospace industry; nearly $1 billion of technology transfer, training, and overseas investment offset transactions represents nearly 24 percent of average annual offset transactions; about 1,800 Explosives Detection Systems machines were procured in 2002; Title III projects have dedicated funds ranging from $88,000 to approximately $164 million; a total of $449.3 million for Title III projects; a $5 million threshold for offset reporting regulations; and the 2004 report covered the 5-year period 1998 through 2002. Figures include '15 C.F.R. Part 700,' '10 C.F.R. Part 216,' '50 U.S.C. App. § 2099,' and '15 C.F.R. Part 701.'

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document recommends that the Secretaries of Agriculture, Health and Human Services, and Transportation, in consultation with the Department of Commerce, develop and implement a system for using the priorities and allocations authority for food and agriculture resources, health resources, and civil transportation respectively. It recommends that the Secretaries of Agriculture, Energy, Health and Human Services, Homeland Security, and Transportation consider, in advance of an emergency, approving programs and placing priority ratings on contracts for items likely to be needed in an emergency. It also recommends that the Secretary of Commerce update regulations to request more specific industry information from prime contractors to improve the assessment of the economic effects of offsets.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that 'a lack of agreement on terminology and differences in views between national defense sectors and government agencies' are challenges identified by participants in the interagency team's consultations. It notes that the interagency working group established a goal of producing a preliminary statement of best practices by the latter half of 2008, but participating nations noted in the report that it will be difficult and time-consuming to do so. It also states that the National Commission on Offsets' final report and recommendations were never produced and no further activity occurred. The document notes that Commerce officials anticipate the outcome of a review of data and methodology to be represented in their next annual report, but changes to the regulation would not affect data collection for the next annual report.

about.text: This document is a GAO report examining the distribution of funds for the Trans-Sahara Counterterrorism Partnership (TSCTP) from 2005 through 2008 and the types of activities supported, as well as the program's implementation, including the extent to which it has been guided by a comprehensive, integrated strategy. It focuses on U.S. counterterrorism efforts in nine partner countries in northwestern Africa.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The document's key findings are: (1) In 2005 through 2007, the key agencies distributed about 74 percent of approximately $230 million obligated to the four countries in the Sahel region, about 3 percent to the Maghreb region, about 8 percent to the sub-Saharan region, and the remaining 15 percent through regional assistance. (2) Several challenges have hampered implementation, including the lack of a comprehensive, integrated strategy; disagreements about whether State should have authority over DOD personnel temporarily assigned to conduct TSCTP activities; fluctuation in the distribution of funds that limited USAID's implementation in Mali; and the lack of common mechanisms for measuring outcomes.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The document states that from 2005 through 2007, the key agencies obligated about $230 million for TSCTP activities, and for 2008, commitments totaled approximately $123 million. In 2005 through 2007, about 74 percent of approximately $230 million was distributed to the Sahel region, about 3 percent to the Maghreb region, and about 8 percent to the sub-Saharan region; the remaining 15 percent was distributed through regional assistance. As of June 2008, the agencies expected to distribute about 49 percent of approximately $123 million committed for 2008 to the Sahel countries, 21 percent to the Maghreb region, 13 percent to the Sub-Saharan countries, and 17 percent for regional assistance. The document also provides specific obligations and commitments by country and year, such as $23 million for Chad in 2005-2007 and $13,570,000 for Mali in 2007.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document recommends that the Secretary of State work through the Director of Foreign Assistance, who serves concurrently as USAID Administrator, to develop a comprehensive strategy for TSCTP in conjunction with the Secretaries of Defense and the Treasury, the U.S. Attorney General, and the heads of any other participating agencies. The strategy should include clear goals, objectives, and milestones, including output and outcome indicators, and identify resources needed to achieve the program's goals. It also recommends that the Secretaries of State and Defense develop and issue joint guidance with regard to DOD personnel temporarily assigned to conduct TSCTP activities in the partner countries.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that the agencies lacked a comprehensive, integrated strategy as of June 2008, and that the planning documents used did not prioritize activities, identify milestones, provide guidance for selecting countries, or define agency roles. It also notes that the agencies had not yet developed common indicators to measure outcomes, and that a classified annex to the report was planned. Additionally, DOD partially concurred with a recommendation, believing sufficient guidance exists, but GAO maintains that joint guidance is needed to resolve disagreements.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report examines how the Chemical Safety and Hazard Investigation Board (CSB) has responded to prior GAO and inspector general recommendations regarding its investigative gap, data quality, human capital, and management problems, and assesses the merits of the current oversight approach using an existing inspector general and alternatives. It concludes that CSB has not fully addressed key recommendations and that problems persist, and recommends actions for CSB and matters for congressional consideration.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: CSB has implemented some GAO and IG recommendations but has not fully addressed several critical recommendations, and problems in governance, management, and oversight persist. Specifically, CSB has not fully responded to recommendations related to investigating more accidents that meet statutory requirements, improving the quality of its accident data, resolving human capital problems, and ensuring accountability and continuity of management. The investigative gap persists: in fiscal year 2007, CSB received notifications of 920 chemical accidents, approximately 35 included at least one fatality, and CSB investigated 1 of these. Data quality problems continue: in a subset of accidents, at least five accidents (about 6 percent) had fatalities not correctly recorded, and seven accidents (about 4 percent) had missing injury data. Human capital problems persist: more employees left CSB in fiscal years 2006 and 2007 than were hired, and the agency has not paid a retention bonus since September 2002. Accountability and management problems continue: CSB lacks a permanent senior executive to manage day-to-day operations. GAO concludes that independent IG oversight remains the most effective option, provided the arrangement is made permanent and funding is provided.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: CSB received notification of approximately 900 chemical accidents in calendar year 2007, and 31 of these were serious or fatal events that warranted CSB investigators. CSB received an appropriation of $9.4 million for fiscal year 2008 and had 39 staff as of January 30, 2008. Since fiscal year 2001, three IGs have made 32 recommendations. In fiscal year 2007, CSB received notifications of 920 chemical accidents; approximately 35 included at least one fatality, and CSB investigated 1 of these. The DHS IG reported in fiscal year 2004 that CSB deployed to 4 of 294 accidents that met statutory criteria, using fiscal year 2002 data. In fiscal year 2006, CSB recorded 822 accidents, deployed to 9, investigated 6, and 38 had fatalities, of which 5 were investigated. In fiscal year 2007, CSB recorded 920 accidents, deployed to 8, investigated 5, and 35 had fatalities, of which 1 was investigated. NTSB's budget is approximately 8 times CSB's budget, and NTSB investigates 250 times as many accidents. In fiscal year 2006, CSB's budget was $9.1 million and NTSB's was $75.9 million; CSB initiated 6 investigations and NTSB initiated 1,521 aviation accident investigations. In fiscal year 2006, CSB reprogrammed compensation funds of $627,891; in fiscal year 2007, $407,383. GAO found at least five accidents (about 6 percent) where fatalities were not correctly recorded and seven accidents (about 4 percent) where injury data were missing. More employees left CSB in fiscal years 2006 and 2007 than were hired: 11 hired (7 noninvestigative staff, 4 investigators) and 14 left (9 noninvestigative staff, 5 investigators). Three of 5 investigators who left were senior investigators with 5 to 7 years of experience. Of the 4 investigators hired, 3 were interns at GS-7 and 1 was a senior investigator at GS-13. In fiscal years 2006 and 2007, 3 of 5 investigators who left were senior investigators. CSB has not paid a retention bonus to any employee since September 2002. In fiscal year 2006, CSB reprogrammed compensation funds of $627,891; in fiscal year 2007, $407,383.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: GAO recommends that the chairman of the Chemical Safety Board develop a plan to address the investigative gap and request the necessary resources from Congress to meet CSB's statutory mandate or seek an amendment to its statutory mandate; consider using the work of other entities, such as government agencies, companies, and contractors (subject to an assessment of the quality of their work) to a greater extent to maximize the board's limited resources; improve the quality of its accident-screening database by better controlling data entry and periodically sampling accident data to evaluate their consistency and completeness; publish a regulation requiring facilities to report all chemical accidents, as required by law, to better inform the agency of important details about accidents that it may not receive from current sources; consider reinstating the position of chief operating officer, with delegations of responsibility for establishing performance goals, holding program managers accountable for meeting those goals, and demonstrating improvement in the agency's ability to meet its statutory mandates over time; and use the Strategic Management of Human Capital portion of the President's Management Agenda to provide criteria for developing a comprehensive human capital plan, with input from investigators that includes specific objectives and performance measures to improve accountability for results and to assist the agency in its goal of improving its human capital and infrastructure. GAO also proposes matters for congressional consideration: Congress may wish to consider amending CSB's authorizing statute or the Inspector General Act of 1978 to permanently give EPA's Inspector General the authority to serve as the oversight body for the agency, and providing the EPA Inspector General with appropriations and staff allocations specifically for the audit function of CSB via a direct line in the EPA appropriation.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: CSB disagreed with GAO's interpretation that the law requires investigation of all accidental releases that result, or have the potential to result, in a fatality, serious injury, or substantial property damage, and stated it would work with Congress to clarify the issue of its statutory mandate and, if appropriate, seek an amendment to its authorizing statute. GAO continues to believe the current law is clear. CSB also disagreed with the recommendation to publish a regulation requiring facilities to report chemical accidents, stating that such a regulation is not needed for the narrow purpose of notifying CSB of major accidents, and that the obligation to collect chemical incident data for broader purposes appears to lie elsewhere in the federal government. CSB questioned the independence of the EPA IG, since CSB issues recommendations to EPA, and disagreed with the matter to permanently give EPA's IG oversight authority. GAO recognized shortcomings with the current EPA IG oversight relationship: the arrangement is not permanent, and EPA IG officials said they have no plans to conduct future program evaluations of CSB. GAO did not evaluate the quality of CSB's investigative products or the quality and effectiveness of its reports, recommendations, and promotion of preventive actions, as those were outside the scope of the mandate.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a GAO report assessing the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation's (PBGC) contracting function. It evaluates the role of contracting in PBGC's mission, the steps taken to improve its acquisition infrastructure and strategic approach, and the improvements to contract oversight processes. The scope covers fiscal years 2000 through 2007 and is a follow-up to GAO's earlier contracting work.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The document finds that contracting plays a central role in helping PBGC achieve its mission and address unpredictable workloads, with PBGC's reliance on contractors outpacing its hiring of federal employees. It finds that PBGC is taking steps to improve its acquisition infrastructure, but its Procurement Department is not yet part of PBGC's strategic decision-making process. It also finds that PBGC has made improvements to contractor oversight and has begun implementing performance-based contracting, which offers potential for better outcomes but also creates new challenges for oversight. The document states that most of PBGC's current contracts lack performance incentives and methods to hold contractors accountable.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The document states that PBGC insures pensions for more than 44 million workers in over 30,000 employer-sponsored defined benefit plans. In fiscal year 2007, roughly 611,000 beneficiaries received over $4.1 billion in benefit payments. PBGC's workforce consists of about 800 federal employees and about 1,500 contract employees. PBGC's budget increased from $165 million in fiscal year 2000 to $398 million in fiscal year 2007. PBGC's contract spending increased from $122 million in fiscal year 2000 to $297 million in fiscal year 2007. Contracting represented 71 percent of PBGC's appropriated budget during this period. In fiscal year 2000, PBGC had 791 contract employees and 763 federal employees. By fiscal year 2007, there were over 1,500 contract employees and 811 federal employees. The number of contract employees peaked in fiscal year 2006 at 1,768. PBGC managed almost 3,800 pension plans with over 1.3 million participants in fiscal year 2007. PBGC has an accumulated deficit of $14 billion for its single-employer program as of September 2007. PBGC manages $68 billion of assets. PBGC had 88 percent more transactions on average and 40 percent more contract dollars on average than four comparable agencies, but had less than half the average number of contracting office staff. PBGC awarded less than $150 million in service contract dollars in fiscal year 2008. Only six of its contracts are performance based, representing a yearly cost of approximately $30 million. PBGC is in the process of awarding an additional $20 million in performance-based contracts. The OMB OFPP memorandum requires a minimum of 40 hours of training to be certified as a COTR. The Procurement Department has an automated customer service questionnaire, which reflects a current customer satisfaction rate of 88 percent.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document recommends that the Director of PBGC revise its strategic plan and, in drafting the corporation's human capital strategic plan, reflect the importance of contracting and PBGC's use of contractors, project its vision of future contractor use, and better link staffing and contracting decisions at the corporate level. It also recommends including the Procurement Department in agency-wide strategic planning, ensuring the Procurement Director sits on PBGC's three strategic teams, broadening the Procurement Department's staffing study, including detailed plans for how contract support will be obtained, assessing contract information, and developing metrics for the annual performance plan. To improve contract management, it recommends providing comprehensive training on performance-based contracting, developing practices to help ensure accountability, and ensuring that future contracts measure performance in terms of outcomes, provide incentives, and ensure payment of award fees only for excellent performance.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that it is still too early to tell what the effect of the new policies will be. It notes that the success of any set of policies will depend on adequate communication across the agency, internal controls, and clear, strong guidance from leadership. The document also notes that PBGC's workload depends on future economic conditions that are difficult to predict. It states that PBGC doesn't foresee large plan terminations and bankruptcies coming in 2008 or 2009, but there are a few plans it is monitoring that could have significant impact. GAO did not conduct an independent assessment of PBGC's staffing study to validate its results. The document also says PBGC is taking steps to avoid common pitfalls in implementing performance-based contracting.

audience.text: This report is addressed to the Chairmen and Ranking Members of the Senate Committee on Finance and the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions, in response to their request for a review of PBGC's contracting function.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report examines how the Department of Defense (DOD) manages its acquisition of tactical radios, focusing on changes in planned investments over fiscal years 2003–2007, the reasons for those changes, and the challenges facing future tactical radio investments. It specifically reviews the shift from investing in the Joint Tactical Radio System (JTRS) to buying legacy radios, and assesses whether DOD has a strategy to balance near-term and long-term needs.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report finds that DOD investments in tactical radios shifted dramatically, with actual spending of about $8.3 billion versus the planned $3.2 billion over fiscal years 2003–2007. This shift was due to JTRS delays and increased demand for legacy radios from combat operations, force modernization, and modularity. Legacy radio spending ballooned to approximately $5.7 billion, while JTRS spending was $2.5 billion with no JTRS networking radios produced. JTRS program restructuring delayed fielding of Ground Mobile Radios by 5 years to 2010, and increased development costs from about $3.5 billion to almost $6 billion. DOD lacks a comprehensive strategy for future tactical radio investments, as previous migration plans are outdated and the waiver/notification process has been ineffective.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: DOD spent an estimated $12 billion on tactical radios over the last 5 years. This is comparable to investments in the Army's Future Combat Systems ($10.4 billion) and the Navy's Virginia Class submarines ($10.8 billion) during the same period. Planned spending for tactical radios between 2003 and 2007 was about $3.2 billion ($0.24 billion legacy, $2.93 billion JTRS); actual spending was about $8.3 billion ($5.72 billion legacy, $2.54 billion JTRS). The Army spent approximately $4.1 billion on legacy radios, including $2.3 billion on SINCGARS and $1.8 billion on handheld/manpack radios; the Marine Corps spent $1.6 billion. Supplemental funding supplied an estimated 90 percent ($5.5 billion out of $6.1 billion) of Army and Marine Corps legacy radio funding. JTRS Ground Mobile Radio production decision was delayed from 2005 to 2010. JTRS development cost increased from about $3.5 billion to almost $6 billion through fiscal year 2011. Army's SINCGARS acquisition objective grew from 232,411 units in fiscal year 2002 to 526,192 in 2007. The Army bought 244,780 SINCGARS between 2003 and 2007. Army planned to spend approximately $310 million between 2005 and 2013 for an alternate helicopter radio. Navy planned to spend approximately $50 million for AN/ARC-210 modernization. JTRS Ground Mobile Radio planned quantities reduced from 108,086 to 86,512 (20 percent decrease); Handheld, Manpack, and Small Form Fit reduced from 328,514 to 95,551 (71 percent decrease); Airborne, Maritime, and Fixed Station reduced from 17,007 to 11,040. A legacy vehicle radio costs about $20,000; a JTRS 4-channel Ground Mobile Radio costs about $220,000. An AN/ARC-210 costs about $80,000; a JTRS 2-channel airborne radio costs about $480,000. cost to retrofit and fully integrate JTRS into four Naval aircraft estimated at about $868 million. JTRS Rifleman Radio preliminary unit cost estimated at about $2,000 versus $8,700 for the small form factor "C" radio.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends that the Secretary of Defense develop a comprehensive strategy and implementation plan for tactical radio investment decisions, based on operational architectures, assessing and prioritizing capabilities, setting funding bounds, laying out a migration and fielding plan, and identifying contingencies for further JTRS delays. It also recommends reinvigorating the tactical radio notification/waiver process to provide department-wide insight into legacy and interim radio procurements. DOD concurred with both recommendations.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report notes that JTRS must still overcome technology hurdles, including size, weight, and power constraints and security architecture issues. It states that whether these technical challenges can be overcome will not be known until major test and evaluation events are conducted. The report also notes that DOD lacks a comprehensive strategy for tactical radio investments and that previous migration plans are outdated. It identifies open questions about how to balance investment between JTRS and legacy radios given cost and the need to phase out legacy radios over 10-15 years.

audience.text: This report is for the U.S. Congress, specifically the Subcommittee on Air and Land Forces of the House Committee on Armed Services, and other oversight committees, to inform decisions on DOD's tactical radio acquisitions.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report (GAO-08-889) examines the status of the construction of a new federal courthouse in Los Angeles, the effects of delays on costs and court operations, and the options available for the future of the project.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report finds that GSA initially estimated in 2000 that the L.A. Court could take occupancy of a new courthouse in fiscal year 2006, but projected occupancy has been delayed by 8 years to fiscal year 2014 at the earliest. The delays have caused the estimated costs for housing the L.A. Court to nearly triple to over $1.1 billion, rendering GSA's currently authorized 41-courtroom courthouse unachievable with currently available funding. The reasons for the project delays include GSA's decision to design a larger courthouse than what was authorized by Congress, slow decision making by GSA and the judiciary to reduce scope and stay on budget, unforeseen cost escalations, and low contractor interest in the project. The report also states that almost half of the courtrooms in the L.A. Court's Spring Street building do not meet the judiciary's standards for size or security, and USMS has chosen not to use the prisoner passageways that exist in the building because they are too dangerous and inefficient.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The report states that GSA has spent $16.3 million designing a new courthouse and $16.9 million acquiring and preparing a new site for it in downtown Los Angeles. Since no construction has occurred, about $366.45 million remains available for the construction of a courthouse in Los Angeles. In 2000, Congress authorized and later funded the design of a new courthouse in Los Angeles, based on a 41-courtroom, 1,016,300-square-foot GSA prospectus. GSA decided instead to design a 54-courtroom, 1,279,650-square-foot building to meet the judiciary's long-term needs. In fiscal year 2001, Congress provided $35.25 million to acquire a site for and design a 41-courtroom building, and in fiscal year 2004, Congress appropriated $50 million for construction of the new L.A. Courthouse. In fiscal year 2005, Congress appropriated $314.4 million for the construction of a new 41-courtroom building in Los Angeles, which Congress designated to remain available until expended for construction of the previously authorized L.A. Courthouse. The report states that GSA estimated that the 41-courtroom courthouse project would cost about $400 million in May 2004, but current estimates for building a new federal courthouse of similar scope now exceed $1.1 billion. At this rate, each day of additional delay costs about $54,000, assuming current escalation rates, according to GSA. Consequently, every 44 days of additional delay cost as much as one 2,400-square-foot district courtroom. The report provides current and projected space deficits in the L.A. Court: court, chamber, and support space current deficit 133,838 square feet and projected 2011 deficit 197,613 square feet; probation current deficit 3,292 square feet and projected 2011 deficit 6,426 square feet; district clerk's office current deficit 6,165 square feet and projected 2011 deficit 25,696 square feet; jury assembly current deficit 9,635 square feet and projected 2011 deficit 9,650 square feet. The report lists three options for housing the L.A. Court currently under consideration: Option 1: Construct a new 36-courtroom, 45-chamber building to house district judges; add 4 more courtrooms to Roybal to house the magistrate and bankruptcy judges; total courtrooms 74; estimated completion date 2014; estimated new appropriations needed $733.6 million. Option 2: Construct a new 20-courtroom, 20-chamber courthouse to house about half of the district judges; add 12 more courtrooms to the Roybal building; total courtrooms 66; estimated completion date 2014; estimated new appropriations needed $301.5 million. Option 3: Add 13 more courtrooms in the Roybal building, retain 17 courtrooms and upgrade security in the Spring Street building, and house the remaining court functions in the federal building on L.A. Street; total courtrooms 64; some below design standards for size; estimated completion date 2016; estimated new appropriations needed $282.1 million.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report explicitly states: 'We are not advocating any of these options. Our intent is to identify current options so that Congress and stakeholders can evaluate them.' It does not make any recommendations.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report notes that the current process is deadlocked, and that there is no consensus among stakeholders on how to proceed. It also notes that GSA's cost estimates for the options assume work would have started by now, which has not occurred for Option 3. The Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts commented that the $1.1 billion figure overstates costs because it includes the cost to overhaul the Roybal building, which was never part of the original $400 million project. The report also notes that the judiciary officials said that the decision to change the scope was made jointly with GSA, while GSA officials disagreed and said that GSA's planning criteria did not contribute to the increase in scope.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a GAO report on the Department of Defense's (DOD) business systems modernization, focusing on the Navy Enterprise Resource Planning (Navy ERP) program. It assesses whether the Department of the Navy is effectively implementing key information technology (IT) management controls—architectural alignment, economic justification, earned value management, requirements management, and risk management—on the program's first increment, and identifies strengths and weaknesses in these areas, along with recommendations for improvement.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report's own findings are: (1) Navy ERP compliance with DOD's federated business enterprise architecture (BEA) has not been sufficiently demonstrated because the compliance assessments omitted relevant architecture products, did not identify potential duplication, did not address the DON enterprise architecture, and were not validated by oversight authorities. (2) The investment is economically justified ($8.6 billion in benefits versus $2.4 billion in costs over a 20-year life cycle), but the cost estimate was not reliably derived because it lacked historical data from comparable programs and a reliable schedule baseline. (3) Earned value management is not effectively implemented because an integrated baseline review has not been performed and industry standards have not been fully implemented or surveilled. (4) An important requirements management activity is effectively implemented, as 58 out of 60 sampled system-level requirements are traceable. (5) A risk management process is defined but not effectively implemented for all risks, particularly those related to data conversion and organizational change management. The report also states that Navy ERP is more than 2 years behind schedule and about $570 million over the original cost estimate.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: Navy ERP is expected to cost approximately $2.4 billion over its 20-year life cycle. The program is to support over 86,000 users. The original life cycle cost estimate in fiscal year 2003 was $1.87 billion, in fiscal year 2004 it was $1.99 billion, and in fiscal year 2007 it was $2.44 billion. The program's cost overrun is about $570 million. The estimated benefits are about $8.6 billion (including $2.7 billion in legacy system cost savings, $3.3 billion from inventory reductions, and $2.7 billion from labor productivity improvements). The program is to retire 138 legacy systems between fiscal years 2005 and 2015, with yearly maintenance costs per system as high as about $39 million. The uncertainty analysis on benefit estimates showed a reduction of only $11 million. The latest estimate to complete budgeted development work for all three releases is about $844 million, with a likely overrun of about $152 million. DON's fiscal year 2008 budget for business systems was about $2.7 billion. About $400 million was spent from fiscal year 2004 through fiscal year 2007 on the first increment, and about $200 million was planned for fiscal year 2008. Release 1.0 provides about 56 percent of Template 1 requirements. The cost estimate increased by about $461 million in December 2006. The integrated baseline review for Release 1.1 was scheduled for August 2008. The Navy ERP cost estimate was within 11 percent of an independent estimate. The program's first increment was originally to reach full operational capability in fiscal year 2011, now planned for fiscal year 2013. Release 1.0 was 22 months later than the August 2004 baseline and 4 months later than the September 2007 baseline. Release 1.0 deployment at SPAWAR is 18 months later than planned (October 2009), and at NAVSEA general fund and Working Capital Fund 12 months later (October 2010 and 2011). Release 1.1 deployment at NAVSUP is 7 months later (February 2010). Full operational capability is 26 months later than the 2004 baseline and 5 months later than the September 2007 re-baseline. BearingPoint contract was $176 million, and IBM contract was $151 million.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document makes recommendations to the Secretary of Defense aimed at addressing cost and schedule estimating, EVM, and risk management weaknesses. Specifically, it recommends improving the program's cost estimates, improving the integrated master schedule, and addressing EVM and risk management weaknesses. The department concurred with two recommendations and partially concurred with two. The document does not make recommendations for addressing architecture compliance weaknesses because separate work was completed on that topic.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that architectural compliance assessments did not include all relevant architecture products, potential duplication across programs was not identified, and compliance with the DON enterprise architecture was not addressed because of policy, guidance, and tool limitations. It also states that benefit estimates were not subject to uncertainty analysis as prescribed by guidance, and the cost estimate was not grounded in historical data from comparable programs or based on a reliable schedule baseline. The document notes that DOD has not established a standardized cost element structure for ERP programs or a repository for historical cost data, which are prerequisites for reliable cost estimation. The document acknowledges that the program has not performed an integrated baseline review for any release, and that independent surveillance of EVM has not occurred. It also notes that the program lacks an integrated master schedule for the entire first increment, which prevents identification of a critical path and performance of a schedule risk analysis. The document states that DOD did not agree with GAO's assessment that certain risks were not reflected in the cost estimate's uncertainty analysis, and offers no new information to counter the report's findings. The document does not settle whether the program will achieve its cost and schedule goals, but indicates that additional cost and schedule overruns are likely without improvements.

audience.text: The report is addressed to the Subcommittee on Readiness and Management Support, Committee on Armed Services, U.S. Senate. It supports oversight and decision-making regarding DOD's business systems modernization, specifically the Navy ERP program.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document, a GAO report issued in July 2008, examines how state and local governments in the five Gulf Coast states (Alabama, Florida, Louisiana, Mississippi, and Texas) allocated and used four federal tax incentives established by the Gulf Opportunity Zone Act of 2005 following Hurricanes Katrina, Rita, and Wilma. It covers the processes for allocation, the amounts allocated and used for each incentive, and the purposes for which they were used, including low-income housing and a wide range of private facilities.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The document finds that state governments were responsible for allocating four tax incentives: $14.9 billion in tax-exempt private activity bonds, $330 million in low-income housing tax credits, $350 million in tax credit bonds, and $7.9 billion in additional advance refunding bonds. As of mid-June 2008, states had allocated about 87 percent of the private activity bond authority and issued bonds for about half of that, reflecting 44 percent of the total. The five states awarded 95 percent of the LIHTC authority. Few planned LIHTC units were in service as of April 2008. Louisiana and Mississippi exhausted their tax credit bond authority, while Alabama did not issue tax credit bonds. The three eligible states used 16 percent of the advance refunding authority. States generally allocated bonds on a first-come, first-served basis without consistently targeting the most damaged areas. State officials identified challenges including reduced credit availability and declining tax credit values.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: $14.9 billion in tax-exempt private activity bond authority; $330 million in low-income housing tax credit allocation; $350 million in GO Zone tax credit bonds; $7.9 billion in additional advance refunding bonds; $2,174 million (Alabama), $7,840 million (Louisiana), $4,921 million (Mississippi) for GO Zone tax-exempt private activity bonds; $47 million (Alabama), $170 million (Louisiana), $106 million (Mississippi) for GO Zone LIHTC; $50 million (Alabama), $200 million (Louisiana), $100 million (Mississippi) for GO Zone tax credit bonds; $1,125 million (Alabama), $4,500 million (Louisiana), $2,250 million (Mississippi) for GO Zone additional advance refunding bonds; $3.5 million in GO Zone LIHTC authority for Florida and Texas each; 87 percent of private activity bond authority allocated as of mid-June 2008; 95 percent of LIHTC authority awarded as of April 2008; 44 percent of total bond authority issued; about $10.4 billion in FEMA Public Assistance as of April 2008; $19.7 billion in HUD CDBG as of May 2008; 17 percent of Louisiana's and 45 percent of Mississippi's major or severe damaged rental units addressed by GO Zone LIHTC units; $300 million in total tax credit bonds issued; $599 million (Alabama), $483 million (Louisiana), $169 million (Mississippi) in advance refunding bonds issued; 53 percent, 11 percent, and 8 percent of advance refunding authority used by Alabama, Louisiana, and Mississippi, respectively; 16 percent of total advance refunding authority used; 74 percent of Alabama's LIHTC allocation awarded; $113 million of additional GO Zone LIHTC allocations awarded by Florida, Mississippi, and Texas.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document does not make recommendations for action. It reports on the allocation and use of tax incentives, noting that officials made technical comments which were incorporated as appropriate, but it does not call for any specific actions or changes.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document notes limitations: County-level data on major and severe damages to rental housing units were not available for Alabama, Florida, or Texas; comparable data were not available for every GO Zone parish and county in Louisiana and Mississippi; the report did not quantify aggregate bond use by categories across states due to differences in reporting; and the report states that the extent to which GO Zone LIHTC units will be in service by the January 1, 2011 deadline is not yet known, as few units were in service as of April 2008. It also notes that state officials were uncertain whether the bonds should be used quickly anywhere in the zone or focused on damaged areas, and that some projects may have been viable without tax-exempt financing.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This is a GAO audit report assessing the Department of Veterans Affairs' progress in strengthening controls over IT equipment, addressing prior recommendations, and evaluating the effectiveness of current controls to prevent theft, loss, or misappropriation. The report covers a follow-up audit conducted from January 2008 through July 2008, including VA's 2007 departmentwide physical inventory and statistical tests at four case study locations.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The document's findings are that VA has made significant progress in addressing GAO recommendations, completing action on 10 of 12 recommendations from the July 2007 report and 4 of 6 property-related recommendations from the July 2004 report. However, VA's 2007 departmentwide physical inventory initially identified approximately 79,000 missing IT equipment items, and as of May 15, 2008, approximately 62,800 recorded items could not be located, of which over 9,800 could have stored sensitive information. Statistical tests at four case study locations identified 50 missing items, 34 of which could have stored sensitive information, with estimated failure rates of 1 percent at Puget Sound HCS, 3 percent at Boston HCS, 6 percent at North Texas HCS, and 12 percent at VA headquarters. Other findings include high failure rates for correct user organization (91% at North Texas, 60% at Boston, 76% at Puget Sound, 12% at headquarters), correct user location (46% at North Texas, 17% at Boston, 14% at Puget Sound, 33% at headquarters), and recordkeeping errors (9% at North Texas, 41% at Boston, 9% at Puget Sound, 4% at headquarters). There were also weaknesses in controls over hard drives in the disposal process and physical security at IT storage locations.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: VA employed over 230,000 individuals during 2007. The 2007 departmentwide physical inventory initially identified approximately 79,000 missing items; as of May 15, 2008, approximately 62,800 recorded items could not be located, of which over 9,800 could have stored sensitive information. The four case study locations had missing items as of May 15, 2008: North Texas HCS 5,308; Puget Sound HCS 1,269; Boston HCS 3,226; VA headquarters 1,314. The estimated inventory control failure rates for missing items were 1% at Puget Sound HCS, 3% at Boston HCS, 6% at North Texas HCS, and 12% for VA headquarters. Blank serial number rates were 59% at North Texas, 17% at Boston, 1% at Puget Sound, and 1% at headquarters. Incorrect user organization rates were 91% at North Texas, 60% at Boston, 76% at Puget Sound, and 12% at headquarters. Incorrect user location rates were 46% at North Texas, 17% at Boston, 14% at Puget Sound, and 33% at headquarters. Recordkeeping error rates were 9% at North Texas, 41% at Boston, 9% at Puget Sound, and 4% at headquarters. The total for missing items at all VA locations was 62,880, with 9,866 open Reports of Survey items that could have stored sensitive data. At the case study locations, missing items that could have stored sensitive information as of May 15, 2008: North Texas HCS 3,351; Puget Sound HCS 443; Boston HCS 725; VA headquarters 608.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends that the Secretary of Veterans Affairs require the CIO, with the support of medical centers and VA headquarters organizations and other VA organizations, to take five actions: (1) review property inventory records and confirm that all IT equipment, regardless of the organizational equipment inventory listing, is identified in the property system; (2) establish and implement a policy requiring development of standardized naming classifications for IT equipment—including item name, manufacturer, and model—for recording into local property inventory systems; (3) develop a list of medical equipment with data storage capability that should be considered as IT equipment for inventory control purposes; (4) develop a procedure for identifying hard drive serial numbers with both the property identification numbers and serial numbers of host computers; and (5) revise the definition of IT storage locations in VA's Handbook 0730/1 to include informal IT storage locations and require these locations to be included in physical security inspections.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document notes that because VA does not know what, if any, sensitive information resided on missing equipment, notifications to potentially affected individuals could not be made. It also states that the numbers of missing items could be higher because not all IT equipment items were included in the departmentwide inventory, such as medical equipment with data storage capabilities and items not accounted for in the OIT equipment inventory listing. The document also notes that it did not validate the results of the VA-wide inventory.

audience.name: Who it is for
audience.text: The report is addressed to the Subcommittee on Oversight and Investigations, Committee on Veterans' Affairs, House of Representatives, and supports congressional oversight of VA IT equipment control.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a GAO report examining the extent of and reasons for rebaselining of major federal information technology (IT) projects, and whether agencies have sound policies for rebaselining projects, based on a survey of 24 major federal agencies.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report's own findings include: an estimated 48 percent of the federal government's major IT projects have been rebaselined; of those, about 51 percent were rebaselined at least twice, and about 11 percent were rebaselined 4 or more times; the most commonly cited reason for rebaselining was changes in project requirements, objectives, or scope (55 percent), and another frequently cited reason was changes in funding stream (44 percent); agencies' rebaselining policies are not comprehensive, with none of the policies fully consistent with best practices; and the Office of Management and Budget has not issued guidance specifying what elements these policies are to include.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The federal government plans to spend about $70 billion on IT projects during fiscal year 2008. The survey covered a random sample of 180 projects from a total of 778 major IT projects, with a 99% response rate. About 48 percent of major IT projects have been rebaselined. Of rebaselined projects, 51 percent were rebaselined at least twice, and about 11 percent were rebaselined 4 or more times. The most commonly cited reason for rebaselining was changes in project requirements, objectives, or scope—55 percent, and another frequently cited reason was changes in funding stream—44 percent. The U.S. Coast Guard's Rescue 21 system is projected to have cost increases of 184 percent and schedule delays of 5 years. None of the policies were fully consistent with best practices. Most policies fully or partially addressed describing reasons for rebaselining (79 percent), requiring management review (96 percent), and requiring that the rebaselining process be documented (88 percent), while describing the process for developing the new baseline and requiring validation were addressed the least (46 percent and 54 percent of the policies, respectively, did not address these practices).

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document recommends that the Director of OMB issue guidance for rebaselining policies that would include a minimum set of key elements, taking into consideration the criteria used in this report, and that each of the heads of the 24 major agencies direct the development of comprehensive rebaselining policies that address the weaknesses identified.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document does not settle the exact extent of rebaselining; estimates are based on a sample with a 95 percent confidence interval of within plus or minus 11 percentage points. It also notes that OMB has not established specific criteria to evaluate agencies' earned value management policies, and that agencies' policies vary in part because no guidance has been issued specifying what elements these policies are to include. The document also notes that the Department of Homeland Security disagreed with the assessment of its policies, but the department did not provide the relevant guidance to support its claim.

audience.text: This report is intended for congressional requesters, specifically the Subcommittee on Federal Financial Management, Government Information, Federal Services, and International Security of the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs of the United States Senate.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report to congressional committees assesses Department of Defense (DOD) planning for the reposturing of U.S. forces from Iraq, focusing on logistical organizations and processes supporting a drawdown, especially the retrograde of materiel and equipment. It covers planning efforts begun in fall 2007 and coordinated in May 2008, the lack of clear roles and responsibilities for retrograde management, and nine issues DOD needs to consider in its planning.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: Key findings include: (1) DOD began planning for reposturing in fall 2007, but efforts were initially uncoordinated until a May 2008 logistics summit and subsequent MNF-I order; (2) planning relies on three assumptions—reposturing based on MNF-I and State Department assessments, sufficient lead time, and a deliberate pace with a 180-day template and a sustained flow of no more than 2.5 brigades' worth of equipment out monthly; (3) DOD has not clearly established roles and responsibilities for retrograde management, as evidenced by lack of authority over theater property and retrograde support teams, no theater command authority over the 401st and 402nd Army Field Support Brigades until June 2008, and incompatible data systems; (4) the retrograde process for theater provided equipment is slow and lacks in-transit visibility due to manual data manipulations; (5) nine issues need consideration: base closures, contractor reposturing, contractor-managed property accountability, Kuwait facility restrictions, wash rack and customs inspector availability, transport and security assets, home station issues (mental health, infrastructure, reset), and more.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: As of April 26, 2008, approximately 149,400 DOD contractors; as of July 1, 2008, approximately 147,400 U.S. troops deployed. Approximately 311 installations, some more than 500 miles from Kuwait. Approximately 80 percent of equipment is theater provided. As of March 2008, theater provided equipment totaled approximately 173,000 major end items worth approximately $16.5 billion. As of May 2008, the equivalent of 47 brigades' worth of materiel, approximately 582,000 pieces of equipment worth about $15.5 billion. As of summer 2007, more than 60,000 materiel containers and over 127,000 short-tons of ammunition in Iraq and Kuwait. In May 2008, 177 pieces of rolling stock sat idle in Kuwait; over 2,100 non-rolling stock items awaiting disposition. At least $3.5 billion in contractor-managed government-owned property; $3.37 billion under LOGCAP. Donation threshold increased from $5,000 to $10,000 in October 2007, and to $15,000 in June 2008. Approximately 85 percent of contractor-acquired government-owned property should be transferred, sold, or scrapped in Iraq. 211 wash racks in Kuwait (81 at Camp Arifjan, 130 at Kuwait Naval Base; 100 useable there). Wash rack operations suspended 6 days each quarter for ammunition loading. Heavy vehicles take 40 to 80 hours to wash; small vehicles 4 to 8 hours. 24 to 48 hours delay for manifest information. 180-day redeployment template. 2.5 brigades' worth of equipment flow per month. 22 organizations participate in the 180-day process. 10 theater property and retrograde support teams.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: The GAO report examines the Department of Veterans Affairs' (VA) progress in reducing underutilized and vacant real property from fiscal years 2005 to 2007, the costs of maintaining such property, the use and tracking of legal authorities (like enhanced-use leases and sharing agreements) to reduce property, and the challenges VA faces in these efforts. It addresses three questions: the extent of reductions and costs, how authorities are used and tracked, and challenges and steps taken. The report is based on analysis of VA data, site visits, and interviews, and includes recommendations for VA.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report's key findings are that VA reduced underutilized space by nearly two-thirds from 15.4 million to 5.6 million square feet from fiscal year 2005 to 2007, but vacant space remained relatively unchanged at about 7.3 million square feet in fiscal year 2007. The estimated cost to operate and maintain underutilized and vacant space at VA medical facilities in fiscal year 2007 was $175 million. VA does not track the cost of operating and maintaining underutilized and vacant space at the building level and lacks a reliable cost estimate. VA also does not track the overall effect of its various legal authorities on space reductions, and it faces challenges such as building location, high repair costs (estimated $3 billion for underutilized and vacant properties), competing stakeholder interests, and legal restrictions. Some locations have used strategies like stakeholder communication and public-private partnerships to mitigate these challenges.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: From fiscal year 2005 through 2007, VA reduced underutilized space from 15.4 million square feet to 5.6 million square feet. Underutilized space accounted for approximately 10 percent of VA's total gross square feet in fiscal year 2005 and less than 4 percent in fiscal year 2007. Vacant space totaled approximately 7.3 million square feet in fiscal year 2007, accounting for 5 percent of total square feet in all 3 fiscal years. VA spent an estimated $175 million operating and maintaining underutilized and vacant space at its medical facilities in fiscal year 2007. The number of underutilized buildings was 2,513 in fiscal year 2006 and 2,381 in fiscal year 2007; vacant buildings numbered 684 in fiscal year 2006 and 482 in fiscal year 2007. In fiscal year 2007, VA had 46 EULs, 185 sharing agreements, and 250 outleases. VA disposed of 91 buildings through EULs, 98 by demolition, 5 sold or donated, and 6 through GSA in fiscal years 2005-2007. Repairs for underutilized and vacant properties were estimated at approximately $3 billion. 56 percent of buildings in poor or critical condition at the end of fiscal year 2007 were underutilized or vacant. 66 percent of underutilized and vacant buildings are historic properties or eligible for historic designation. In fiscal year 2007, VHA had 2,716 available acres, an increase from 2,356 acres in fiscal year 2005. The independent cost estimate ranged from $175 million to $185 million at the 50 percent and 70 percent confidence levels. VA spent $3,449,568 demolishing 44 buildings totaling 216,952 square feet in fiscal year 2007.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends that the Secretary of Veterans Affairs take three actions: (1) develop an annual cost estimate for how much VA spends on underutilized and vacant property, so that the estimate is comprehensive, accurate, well-documented, and credible; (2) collect and maintain building-level data by fiscal year in order to correlate characteristics associated with underutilized and vacant buildings, which may help identify unneeded assets; and (3) track, monitor, and evaluate square footage reductions and financial and nonfinancial benefits when recording new agreements as of fiscal year 2008.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document notes that VA does not track the overall effect of its authorities on space reductions, and lacks building-level data prior to fiscal year 2006, preventing trend analyses and correlations between utilization and location, condition, and age. It also states that the accuracy of its cost estimate depends on VA's data, and that data errors and reporting deficiencies exist; VA is completing an audit of the Capital Asset Inventory database that could affect the estimate. VA did not concur with one recommendation, and the report acknowledges areas of disagreement with VA's comments.

audience.name: Who it is for
audience.text: The report is addressed to the Ranking Member, Committee on Veterans' Affairs, House of Representatives.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This is a GAO report (GAO-08-954) issued July 28, 2008, to congressional requesters. It describes the progress of the Department of Defense and the Department of Veterans Affairs in developing electronic health record systems or capabilities that allow for full interoperability of personal health care information between the departments, steps taken to ensure compliance with applicable federal interoperability standards, and efforts to set up the joint interagency program office. The report is semi-annual, as required by the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2008.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report's findings are that DOD and VA have established and implemented mechanisms to achieve interoperable sharing of some, but not all, electronic health information; pharmacy and drug allergy data on about 18,300 shared patients are exchanged at the highest level of interoperability (computable form), while other data such as microbiology results, cytology reports, and chemistry and hematology reports are shared at a viewable level. Not all electronic health information is shared, including immunization records and history, data on exposure to health hazards, and psychological health treatment and care records. Many DOD medical facilities use paper-based health records. DOD and VA have agreed upon numerous common standards, and the joint interagency program office is not yet fully established, lacking permanent leadership, staff, and facilities; the implementation plan is in draft with several milestone dates undetermined, even though all capabilities are to be achieved by September 2009.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: about 18,300 shared patients as of June 2008; September 30, 2009 (deadline for full interoperability); February 28, 2008 (due date for schedules and benchmarks); April 25 (draft implementation plan date); April 17, 2008 (appointment of Acting Director and Deputy Director); about 30 (expected permanent staff); $4.94 million for fiscal year 2008; $6.94 million for fiscal year 2009; 52 milestone dates for Interoperability II, 19 yet to be determined; October 2008, December 2008, July 31, 2008, October 31, 2008 (various planned dates); 17 DOD sites (about 40% of inpatient beds); 37 ambulatory products certified in 2006; 100+ products certified to date; 20 sets of standards endorsed under Consolidated Health Informatics; 700 existing standards examined; 30 named standards identified; 5 interoperability specifications recognized or released (IS 01–IS 07 statuses); 1 year (implementation testing period); 2001, 2004, 2005, 2007, 2008 (various years); 9 months (remaining after office fully set up); 2 stages (Interoperability I and II); 7 use cases developed in 2006 and 2007; 6 use cases for 2008; 2004 (executive order); 2014 (widespread adoption goal); version 3.3 of AHLTA; 3 DOD locations for beta testing; 1 year (between acceptance and recognition).

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends that the Secretaries of Defense and Veterans Affairs give priority to fully establishing the Joint Interagency Program Office by expediting efforts to put in place permanent leadership, staff, and facilities, and make the necessary decisions to finalize the draft implementation plan.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report states that not all electronic health information is shared; the number of shared patients currently receiving care is unknown; the DOD/VA Information Interoperability Plan has not been finalized and has not been assessed by GAO; milestone dates for Interoperability II enhancements are not fully established; the office's scope may broaden, affecting staffing; the departments have not yet decided on a joint system for inpatient health records; the report notes that HHS's June 2008 strategic plan has not been fully assessed; and the report notes that clinical encounters for TRICARE enrollees are not captured unless care is at a military treatment facility.

audience.name: Who it is for
audience.text: The report is addressed to the congressional committees of jurisdiction, including the Committees on Appropriations, Armed Services, and Veterans' Affairs of both the Senate and the House of Representatives. It supports their oversight of DOD and VA progress toward fully interoperable electronic health records, as required by the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2008.

about.text: This GAO report describes covert testing of Medicare's durable medical equipment (DMEPOS) supplier screening process. It details how GAO created fictitious companies, obtained Medicare billing numbers, and completed electronic test billing, exposing weaknesses in oversight that allowed fraudulent suppliers to enter the program.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: CMS approved both fictitious DMEPOS storefronts despite having no clients or inventory. NSC performed limited verification, accepting phony wholesaler contracts. GAO successfully completed test billing for the Virginia office. Case studies from HHS IG show fraudulent suppliers billed and were paid millions.
