about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a GAO report (GAO-08-976, issued September 11, 2008) on the Veterans Health Administration's (VHA) use of miscellaneous obligations during fiscal year 2007. It reviews how VHA used miscellaneous obligations and whether VA's policies and procedures were designed to provide adequate controls over their authorization and use.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report's key findings are that in fiscal year 2007, VHA used miscellaneous obligations to record over $6.9 billion against its appropriations, and that VA policies and procedures were not designed to provide adequate controls over their use with respect to oversight by contracting officials, segregation of duties, and supporting documentation. These control design flaws increase the risk of fraud, waste, and abuse. The report confirms these weaknesses at three case study locations (Pittsburgh, Cheyenne, and Kansas City).

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: Nearly 132,000 miscellaneous obligations were created, with a total value of nearly $9.8 billion. VHA used approximately $6.9 billion in miscellaneous obligations (about 70% of the total), while VA's Central Office used $2.9 billion (30%). Of VHA's total, almost $3.8 billion (55.1%) was for fee-based medical and dental services, and $1.4 billion (20.4%) was for drugs, medicines, and hospital supplies. Over 88,000 (69%) of 127,070 miscellaneous obligations did not include vendor information, accounting for over $5 billion of the $6.9 billion. In case studies, 42 obligations totaling $36,045,896 were reviewed; none had documented approval by contracting officials, 30 had inadequate segregation of duties, 8 had incomplete purpose descriptions, 20 had blank vendor fields, and 16 had blank contract fields. In fiscal year 2007, VA received appropriations of over $77 billion, including over $35 billion for health care and approximately $41.4 billion for other benefits.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report makes four recommendations to VA: establish a process for the review of miscellaneous obligations by contracting officials, including requiring appropriate documentation that the review has occurred; segregate duties for (1) creating, approving, and recording miscellaneous obligations, (2) the certification and payment of invoices, and (3) the receipt of the resulting goods or services; document the purposes, vendors, and contract numbers of miscellaneous obligations; and establish an oversight mechanism to ensure that these control policies and procedures are fully and effectively implemented.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report states that the 42 obligations reviewed were a nongeneralizable sample and results cannot be projected to the overall population of miscellaneous obligations. It also notes that the review did not include VHA's procurement or service authorization processes, and that while no examples of fraudulent or otherwise improper purchases were found, the work was not designed to identify such cases or estimate their full extent. The report also notes that it could not verify that VHA officials were properly following the fee schedule for payments to non-VA physicians.

audience.name: Who it is for
audience.text: This report is addressed to the Subcommittee on Oversight and Investigations, Committee on Veterans' Affairs, House of Representatives, and is intended to inform congressional oversight of VHA's financial management and controls.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report examines DOD's programs to promote positive working relationships between reservists and their employers, specifically assessing steps taken to inform reservists of their obligations to notify employers, initiatives to promote positive relations, and whether there has been a reduction in hiring of reservists since September 11, 2001.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: DOD has taken steps to inform reservists of their obligations and responsibilities to their civilian employers when mobilized, but it does not collect data to assess the effectiveness of its efforts. DOD has used ESGR as its focal point in establishing a strategic approach to promote positive working relationships, but it does not measure the efficiency and effectiveness of these efforts. The report was unable to determine the extent of any reduction in hiring of reservists caused by increased use or policy changes after September 11, 2001, due to lack of data.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: More than 650,000 members of the National Guard and Reserve have supported operations since September 11, 2001. In fiscal year 2007, more than 67,000 employers and approximately 235,000 reservists were briefed on USERRA and ESGR services. An estimated 79 percent of those responding to a 2006 DOD SOFS said they had been briefed on USERRA at least once. According to the 2007 SOFS, an estimated 76 percent of reservists had received an informal alert notice; of those, an estimated 77 percent received notice of 30 days or more. An estimated 47 percent of reservists reported on the 2007 SOFS that they received written, formal orders 30 days or more prior to having to report for active duty. During fiscal year 2007, more than 20,644 employers signed statements of support. In fiscal year 2007, ESGR field committees briefed 68,803 employers. During fiscal year 2007, 15,124 employers were nominated for the Patriot Award. In fiscal year 2007, more than 1,000 reservists nominated their employers for the Freedom Award. A November 2007 DOD report to Congress found that nearly 70 percent of employers of selected reservists have fewer than 100 employees. For fiscal year 2008, ESGR has a budget of approximately $13.1 million. ESGR has 36 military employees, 28 civilian employees, 8 contractors, and 94 contractor field support personnel. It operates through a network of more than 4,500 volunteers throughout 56 committees.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends that the Secretary of Defense direct the Under Secretary of Defense for Personnel and Readiness to (1) establish an annual performance plan, (2) conduct regular and recurring follow-up activities, and (3) develop initiatives to outreach to small businesses.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report states it was unable to determine the extent to which there has been a reduction in the hiring of reservists caused by the increase in the use of reservists after September 11, 2001, or caused by any changes in DOD's policies, due to a lack of available data. It also notes that the results from focus groups and interviews are not generalizable due to nonprobability sampling.

audience.name: Who it is for
audience.text: This report is intended for the Senate Committee on Armed Services, the Senate Committee on Small Business and Entrepreneurship, the House Committee on Armed Services, and the House Committee on Small Business.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a GAO report on continuing debris removal and disposal issues in the New Orleans area following Hurricane Katrina. It describes key plans and practices federal and state agencies use to oversee debris removal and disposal, enforcement actions related to debris removal and disposal, and actions by LDEQ and EPA in response to potential environmental issues at the Gentilly Landfill.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: Key findings include the continuing slow pace of home demolitions, with an estimated 6,100 homes remaining to be demolished around the New Orleans area as of July 2008. LDEQ had issued 120 enforcement actions by May 15, 2008, including actions against five C&D landfills that received Katrina debris. A disaster debris reduction pilot project in St. Bernard Parish was scaled back to exclude regulated asbestos-containing material due to community concerns and an acknowledged error in EPA's risk estimate.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: More than 1,600 people lost their lives and more than a million were driven from their homes. FEMA estimated in July 2008 that it had funded about 16,900 home demolitions, with an estimated 6,100 homes remaining. More than 100 million cubic yards of disaster debris will have been generated. As of May 15, 2008, LDEQ had issued 120 enforcement actions. EPA and LDEQ have conducted 3,364 landfill observations at 13 sites since October 2005. The agencies have observed demolition activities at 8,706 residences since March 2006. EPA has monitored for asbestos emissions at 300 demolitions since August 2007. LDEQ indicated that 12,000 residence demolitions had been completed by February 2007, and by July 2008, only another 5,000 had been completed.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: This document makes no new recommendations. It encourages EPA to expeditiously complete its responses to all of the recommendations from the prior 2007 report and to carefully consider the continued need to waive certain aspects of the Clean Air Act's asbestos requirements for building demolitions and to work with LDEQ as it considers whether it is necessary to continue to allow carpeting and furniture into some C&D landfills.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report notes that final closure activities at the Chef Menteur Landfill have not yet been performed and that the Corps of Engineers had not provided a time frame for issuance of a permit as of the end of May 2008. It also states that LDEQ expects to complete an overall summary of the Operation Cleansweep effort by the end of the summer of 2008. The report says it did not evaluate the technical merits of the draft report on the Gentilly Landfill or the effectiveness of LDEQ's responses.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report examines the current processes that domestic air carriers use to conduct watch-list matching for domestic flights, addressing TSA's requirements for air carriers to match passenger information against the No Fly and Selectee lists and the extent to which TSA has assessed air carriers' compliance with those requirements. The report is a public version of a restricted report (GAO-08-453SU) and focuses on TSA's enhanced oversight actions in 2008 and its expectation that Secure Flight will be the ultimate solution.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report finds that prior to April 2008, TSA's security directives for watch-list matching were broad, allowing air carriers discretion in similar-name matching, which led to inconsistent processes and varying effectiveness across carriers. In April 2008, TSA revised the No Fly List security directive to establish a baseline capability for similar-name matching to which all air carriers must conform, and TSA planned to similarly revise the Selectee List security directive. Until a January 2008 special emphasis inspection, TSA had conducted limited testing of air carriers' similar-name-matching capability; the inspection found that no air carrier was successful in identifying matches involving all types of name variations. TSA documented incidents where air carriers failed to identify individuals on the No Fly List, leading to false negative results on international flights, and noted the difficulty in determining the extent of such failures on domestic flights. TSA expects Secure Flight, with implementation beginning in early 2009, to provide a more robust matching capability.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: Approximately 70 percent of all passengers that boarded domestic flights in 2005 were accounted for by the 14 air carriers interviewed. TSA found air carriers in compliance in 1,133 (99 percent) of 1,145 watch-list-related inspections in fiscal year 2007; of these, 1,109 inspections were by transportation security inspectors and 36 by principal security inspectors. Available records referenced name-matching tests in 55 of the 1,109 inspections by transportation security inspectors and in 6 of the 36 inspections by principal security inspectors. As of January 2008, 9 principal security inspectors were responsible for assessing domestic air carriers' compliance; for fiscal year 2007, 72 domestic air carriers were subject to the security directives. As of June 2008, 681 transportation security inspectors were responsible for 459 commercial airports. The January 2008 special emphasis inspection tested 83 air carriers, covering 52 domestic and 31 foreign air carriers, using 100 names on the No Fly List. A May 2008 special emphasis assessment covered seven air carriers. TSA officials estimated air carriers would need 2 to 4 weeks to implement new requirements under the revised security directive. Six of TSA's 9 principal security inspectors stated their assessments did not include certain basic types of similar-name comparisons.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document does not make recommendations. It reports TSA's actions and plans: TSA revised the No Fly List security directive in April 2008 to establish a baseline capability for similar-name matching and planned to revise the Selectee List security directive similarly; it planned to assess air carriers' progress after 30 days and revise the annual inspection plan for transportation security inspectors; it planned to update internal inspection guidance to emphasize testing; and it intended to deploy Secure Flight beginning in January 2009 as the ultimate solution.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states it is too early to determine the extent to which TSA will assess air carriers' compliance with watch-list-matching requirements moving forward, as efforts are still underway. TSA officials acknowledged the new baseline capability does not address all vulnerabilities identified by TSA, and TSA was not able to provide data or analysis to support its assertion that requiring comparisons beyond the baseline was not warranted. GAO did not undertake an independent analysis to determine the sufficiency of the newly established baseline. Results from the 2005 special emphasis assessment are not generalizable due to non-random sampling, and GAO did not assess the reliability of data from the January 2008 special emphasis inspection or the May 2008 special emphasis assessment.
